---
title: "Fundamentals of Atomic Layer Processing"
---

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Learning outcomes
After this chapter you should be able to:

1. Write the rate equations for adsorption and desorption, derive the Langmuir isotherm and the saturation curve from them, and explain why the two are not the same thing.
2. Explain why a saturated half-cycle deposits only a fraction of a monolayer, and why a constant GPC across a temperature range neither proves nor is required for self-limiting growth.
3. Classify a ligand as L or X, predict from bond polarity and the chelate effect how it will behave, and place it in a ligand family.
4. List what a precursor and a second precursor must do, and explain what each requirement rules out.
5. Read a TGA trace and a DSC trace, define T~V~ and T~D~, and calculate a thermal figure of merit.
6. Use residual mass, step size, DTG shape, sample mass and isothermal runs to decide whether, and how, a precursor decomposes in a TGA.
7. Recognize the classic organometallic reaction steps (association, dissociation, reductive elimination, oxidative addition, migratory insertion, ligand exchange) in a surface reaction.
8. Describe how hydroxylated, metal and hydride surfaces differ as nucleation sites, and explain why defects control the first cycles of growth.
:::

This chapter collects the ideas that every atomic layer process depends on. ALD, MLD, ALE and ASD all use self-limiting gas–surface reactions, all use the same families of precursors, and all fail in the same ways when a precursor decomposes or a surface does not cooperate. The later chapters on each process link back here rather than repeating this material. Each section starts with a line saying which processes it applies to.

Most of the examples come from ALD, because that is where the chemistry is best understood. TMA/H~2~O is the model system throughout; its two half-reactions and one full cycle are set out in @sec-tma-model.

## Saturation and surface kinetics {#sec-saturation}

[Applies to: ALD · MLD · ALE · ASD]{.applies}

Self-limitation is the property that makes a process "atomic layer" (@sec-what-makes-ald). This section treats it as what it is: a question of kinetics at a surface. The derivations follow Chapter 2 of @Barry2022.

### Adsorption, desorption and surface energy {#sec-ka-kd}

A clean surface is a high-energy state. Its atoms have lost neighbours on one side, so they are coordinatively unsaturated, and almost anything that bonds to them lowers the surface free energy. That is the driving force for adsorption. The cost is entropy: a molecule that adsorbs loses most of its translational freedom. Adsorption is therefore favoured at low temperature and desorption at high temperature, and the balance between the two is set by two rate constants.

Write the adsorption of a gaseous precursor A onto a free surface site ‖ and its desorption as two elementary steps [@Barry2022]:

$$
\| + \text{A} \xrightarrow{\;k_\text{a}\;} \|\text{A} \qquad\qquad \|\text{A} \xrightarrow{\;k_\text{d}\;} \| + \text{A}
$$ {#eq-ads-steps}

Adsorption is second order (it needs a molecule and a free site) and desorption is first order. Define the coverage θ as the fraction of sites occupied, so that 1 − θ is the fraction free, and express the amount of A as its partial pressure p~A~. The two rates are then

$$
R_\text{a} = k_\text{a}\,p_\text{A}\,(1-\theta) \qquad\qquad R_\text{d} = k_\text{d}\,\theta
$$ {#eq-rates}

Both rate constants depend on temperature. Desorption is thermally activated, with an activation energy close to the adsorption energy E~des~, so the average time a molecule stays on the surface (its *residence time*) is

$$
\tau = \frac{1}{k_\text{d}} = \tau_0 \exp\!\left(\frac{E_\text{des}}{RT}\right)
$$ {#eq-residence}

where τ~0~ is roughly one vibrational period, about 10^−13^ s. This is where the difference between physisorption and chemisorption (@sec-vocabulary) becomes quantitative. At 200 °C, a physisorbed molecule held by 40 kJ mol^−1^ stays for a few nanoseconds. A chemisorbed fragment held by 150 kJ mol^−1^ stays for about an hour, far longer than any cycle. Physisorption can be the first step towards chemisorption, but a physisorbed layer starts to desorb as soon as the pulse ends and the gas-phase pressure drops, so it cannot by itself give a self-limiting step [@Barry2022].

The monolayer does not have to be thermodynamically stable. It has to be *kinetically* stable: it must last longer than the purge and the next dose. Once a ligand has left as a by-product and been pumped away, the surface fragment has no easy route back to the gas phase, which is why chemisorption by ligand loss is effectively irreversible under process conditions [@Barry2022].

### The Langmuir isotherm {#sec-langmuir}

If adsorption and desorption are left to reach equilibrium, R~a~ = R~d~ and

$$
\theta_\text{eq} = \frac{k_\text{a}p_\text{A}}{k_\text{a}p_\text{A} + k_\text{d}} = \frac{K p_\text{A}}{1 + K p_\text{A}}, \qquad K = \frac{k_\text{a}}{k_\text{d}}
$$ {#eq-isotherm}

This is the Langmuir isotherm. It describes how much of the surface is covered at infinite time for a given pressure, and it shows that full coverage (θ~eq~ → 1) needs adsorption to dominate desorption, k~a~p~A~ ≫ k~d~ [@Barry2022]. The isotherm assumes identical, independent sites, an ideal gas and one adsorbate per site. Real surfaces break all three assumptions, but the isotherm is still the right starting point.

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.1: Langmuir coverage and residence time]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof lgmT = Inputs.range([25, 450], {value: 200, step: 5, label: "Temperature (°C)"})
viewof lgmE = Inputs.range([20, 200], {value: 140, step: 1, label: "Desorption energy, E_des (kJ mol⁻¹)"})
viewof lgmKa = Inputs.range([0, 5], {value: 2.7, step: 0.1, label: "log₁₀ kₐ (Torr⁻¹ s⁻¹)"})
viewof lgmP = Inputs.range([-5, -1], {value: -2, step: 0.1, label: "log₁₀ partial pressure (Torr)"})
viewof lgmPurge = Inputs.range([0.1, 30], {value: 5, step: 0.1, label: "Purge time (s)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
lgm = {
  const R = 8.314, tau0 = 1e-13, ka = 10 ** lgmKa;
  const kd = T => (1 / tau0) * Math.exp(-lgmE * 1000 / (R * (T + 273.15)));
  const theta = (p, T) => ka * p / (ka * p + kd(T));
  const ps = d3.range(-7, 0.01, 0.05).map(x => 10 ** x);
  const temps = [lgmT - 50, lgmT, lgmT + 50].filter(T => T >= 0);
  const lines = temps.flatMap(T => ps.map(p => ({p, T: `${T} °C`, th: theta(p, T)})));
  const p = 10 ** lgmP, k = kd(lgmT);
  return {lines, temps, p, kd: k, tau: 1 / k, K: ka / k, th: theta(p, lgmT),
          survive: Math.exp(-k * lgmPurge), t95: Math.log(20) / (ka * p + k)};
}

Plot.plot({
  height: 320, marginLeft: 60, marginBottom: 50, marginTop: 20,
  x: {label: "Partial pressure (Torr) →", type: "log", domain: [1e-7, 1], tickFormat: "~e"},
  y: {label: "↑ Equilibrium coverage, θ_eq", domain: [0, 1.02], grid: true},
  color: {domain: lgm.temps.map(T => `${T} °C`), range: ["#8C8C8C", "#000000", "#E91C24"].slice(0, lgm.temps.length), legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(lgm.lines, {x: "p", y: "th", stroke: "T", strokeWidth: d => d.T === `${lgmT} °C` ? 2.5 : 1.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([lgm.p], {stroke: "#4D4D4D", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),
    Plot.dot([{p: lgm.p, th: lgm.th}], {x: "p", y: "th", r: 6, fill: "#E91C24"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const fmt = t => t < 1e-6 ? `${(t * 1e9).toPrecision(2)} ns` : t < 1e-3 ? `${(t * 1e6).toPrecision(2)} µs`
    : t < 1 ? `${(t * 1e3).toPrecision(2)} ms` : t < 3600 ? `${t.toPrecision(2)} s`
    : t < 86400 * 365 ? `${(t / 3600).toPrecision(2)} h` : "> 1 year";
  const sci = x => { if (x >= 0.01 && x < 1e4) return x.toPrecision(2); const e = Math.floor(Math.log10(x));
    return `${(x / 10 ** e).toFixed(1)}×10${String(e).replace(/[-0-9]/g, c => "⁻⁰¹²³⁴⁵⁶⁷⁸⁹"["-0123456789".indexOf(c)])}`; };
  return md`k_d = **${sci(lgm.kd)} s⁻¹** · residence time τ = **${fmt(lgm.tau)}** · K = **${sci(lgm.K)} Torr⁻¹**

Coverage at this pressure: **θ_eq = ${lgm.th.toFixed(3)}**, reached to 95 % in **${fmt(lgm.t95)}**.
After a ${lgmPurge} s purge, **${(100 * lgm.survive).toFixed(lgm.survive > 0.995 ? 1 : 0)} %** of the adsorbed layer is still there.`
}
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** Langmuir adsorption on identical, independent sites with one molecule per site; desorption follows @eq-residence with τ~0~ = 10^−13^ s and an activation energy equal to E~des~; k~a~ is held constant with temperature (in reality it is often activated too). The "after the purge" figure assumes the gas-phase pressure drops to zero instantly and that desorption is the only loss. The default k~a~ corresponds roughly to TMA at 200 °C with a sticking probability of 10^−3^ (see @sec-dose).

**Things to try.** Lower E~des~ to 110 kJ mol^−1^: the coverage is still high during the pulse, but the layer is lost during the purge. Drop it to physisorption values (20–50 kJ mol^−1^) and the isotherm moves off the plot to high pressure. Raise the temperature at fixed E~des~ and watch the isotherm shift right, which is the high-temperature desorption edge of the ALD window (@sec-ald-window).
:::
:::

### The saturation curve {#sec-saturation-curve}

The Langmuir isotherm is often quoted as the "saturation curve", but that is not correct [@Barry2022]. The isotherm describes equilibrium at infinite time. An ALD pulse lasts milliseconds to seconds, and what matters is how θ grows during it. Combining the two rates in @eq-rates gives

$$
\frac{d\theta}{dt} = k_\text{a}p_\text{A}(1-\theta) - k_\text{d}\,\theta
$$

which integrates, from a bare surface at t = 0, to

$$
\theta(t) = \theta_\text{eq}\left[1 - e^{-(k_\text{a}p_\text{A} + k_\text{d})\,t}\right]
$$ {#eq-saturation}

When adsorption dominates (k~d~ → 0), θ~eq~ → 1 and @eq-saturation reduces to θ ≈ 1 − exp(−k~a~p~A~t) [@Barry2022]. Three things follow:

- **Pressure and time play the same role.** In the irreversible limit, only the product p~A~t appears. This is the *exposure*, usually measured in langmuirs (1 L = 10^−6^ Torr s). Plotting GPC against pulse time is a shortcut that assumes the precursor pressure is constant; exposure is the variable that actually matters [@Barry2022].
- **Saturation does not need irreversibility.** With k~d~ > 0, the curve still reaches a plateau, but more slowly and at θ~eq~ < 1. A process can be perfectly self-limiting while its "monolayer" is only a fraction of the sites. This is one reason why metal ALD often has a GPC far below the thickness of a monolayer of the metal [@Barry2022]. It also means that a small change in vapour pressure can change the coverage a lot when θ~eq~ is well below 1.
- **Two surfaces can saturate at different rates.** If a hydroxylated oxide reacts with rate constant k~a~ and a neighbouring metal with k~a~′ = k~a~/100, then at short pulses the oxide is saturated while the metal has barely reacted. Given long enough, both saturate. This *kinetic selectivity* is a starting point for area-selective deposition [@Barry2022].

In practice, a process is shown to be self-limiting by measuring a saturation curve for **each** precursor and each purge at the temperature of interest: the GPC must plateau as each dose increases, and must stop changing once each purge is long enough. A saturation curve is the only valid demonstration of self-limiting behaviour [@Barry2022].

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.2: Saturation curve builder]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sbKa = Inputs.range([0, 5], {value: 2.7, step: 0.1, label: html`log₁₀ k<sub>a</sub> (Torr⁻¹ s⁻¹)`})
viewof sbP = Inputs.range([0.5, 100], {value: 10, step: 0.5, label: "Partial pressure (mTorr)"})
viewof sbIrr = Inputs.toggle({label: html`Irreversible (k<sub>d</sub> = 0)`, value: false})
viewof sbKd = Inputs.range([-4, 1], {value: -1, step: 0.1, label: html`log₁₀ k<sub>d</sub> (s⁻¹)`})
viewof sbGpc = Inputs.range([0.2, 2], {value: 1.1, step: 0.05, label: "GPC at full coverage (Å)"})
viewof sbSel = Inputs.range([0, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: html`Second surface: log₁₀ (k<sub>a</sub> / k<sub>a</sub>′) (0 = off)`})
viewof sbLog = Inputs.toggle({label: "Logarithmic time axis", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sbNow = {
  const ka = 10 ** sbKa, p = sbP * 1e-3, kd = sbIrr ? 0 : 10 ** sbKd;
  const curve = (kaX) => {
    const r = kaX * p + kd, th = kaX * p / r;
    return t => th * (1 - Math.exp(-r * t));
  };
  const f1 = curve(ka), f2 = curve(ka / 10 ** sbSel);
  const r1 = ka * p + kd, t99 = Math.log(100) / r1;
  return {ka, p, kd, f1, f2, t99, thEq: ka * p / r1,
          label: `kₐ=${ka.toExponential(1)}, p=${sbP} mTorr, k_d=${sbIrr ? 0 : kd.toExponential(1)}`};
}
mutable sbPinned = []
viewof sbPin = Inputs.button([
  ["Pin this curve", () => { mutable sbPinned = [...mutable sbPinned, {f: sbNow.f1, label: sbNow.label}].slice(-5); }],
  ["Clear pinned curves", () => { mutable sbPinned = []; }]
])
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const tMax = Math.max(4 * sbNow.t99, 0.01), tMin = tMax / 1e4;
  const ts = sbLog ? d3.range(0, 201).map(i => tMin * (tMax / tMin) ** (i / 200)) : d3.range(0, 201).map(i => tMax * i / 200);
  const pts = (f, name) => ts.map(t => ({t, g: sbGpc * f(t), name}));
  const data = [
    ...sbPinned.flatMap((c, i) => pts(c.f, `pinned ${i + 1}`)),
    ...(sbSel > 0 ? pts(sbNow.f2, "second surface") : []),
    ...pts(sbNow.f1, "current")
  ];
  const names = [...sbPinned.map((c, i) => `pinned ${i + 1}`), ...(sbSel > 0 ? ["second surface"] : []), "current"];
  const greys = ["#BFBFBF", "#A6A6A6", "#8C8C8C", "#737373", "#595959"];
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 340, marginLeft: 60, marginBottom: 50, marginTop: 20,
    x: {label: "Pulse time (s) →", type: sbLog ? "log" : "linear", domain: sbLog ? [tMin, tMax] : [0, tMax], tickFormat: sbLog ? "~e" : undefined},
    y: {label: "↑ GPC (Å)", domain: [0, sbGpc * 1.1], grid: true},
    color: {domain: names, range: [...greys.slice(0, sbPinned.length), ...(sbSel > 0 ? ["#E91C24"] : []), "#000000"], legend: names.length > 1},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([sbGpc], {stroke: "#8C8C8C", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.line(data, {x: "t", y: "g", stroke: "name", strokeWidth: d => d.name === "current" ? 2.5 : 1.5})
    ]
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const t = sbNow.t99, th1 = sbNow.f1(t), th2 = sbNow.f2(t);
  const S = (th1 - th2) / (th1 + th2);
  const fmt = x => x < 1 ? `${(1000 * x).toPrecision(3)} ms` : `${x.toPrecision(3)} s`;
  return md`Plateau: **${(sbNow.thEq * sbGpc).toFixed(2)} Å** (θ<sub>eq</sub> = ${sbNow.thEq.toFixed(3)}) · Pulse for 99 % of the plateau: **${fmt(t)}** · Exposure at that point: **${(sbNow.p * t / 1e-6).toExponential(1)} L**
${sbSel > 0 ? `\nAt that pulse the second surface has GPC **${(sbGpc * th2).toFixed(2)} Å**, a kinetic selectivity S = (θ₁ − θ₂)/(θ₁ + θ₂) = **${S.toFixed(2)}**.` : ""}`;
}
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** @eq-saturation at constant temperature and constant precursor pressure, with GPC taken as proportional to the coverage of this half-reaction (the other half-reaction is assumed saturated). The "second surface" has the same k~d~ and a smaller k~a~. Not a process model: real reactors deplete the precursor as it reacts, have non-uniform pressure and carrier-gas effects, and produce by-products that can re-adsorb [@Barry2022].

**Things to try.** Pin an irreversible curve, then switch on k~d~ and raise it until it is comparable to k~a~p: the plateau drops and arrives later. Turn on the second surface at log₁₀(k~a~/k~a~′) = 2 and use the logarithmic time axis to see both surfaces saturate eventually.
:::
:::

### Estimating the saturating dose {#sec-dose}

How much precursor is "enough"? For a planar surface, a first estimate comes from kinetic gas theory. The impingement flux of molecules of mass $m$ at pressure $p$ and temperature $T$ is the Hertz–Knudsen flux:

$$
\Phi = \frac{p}{\sqrt{2\pi m k_\mathrm{B} T}}
$$ {#eq-flux}

If each impinging molecule reacts with probability $s$ on a free site, and there are $n_0$ reactive sites per unit area, first-order (Langmuir) kinetics give the fractional coverage after a pulse of length $t$:

$$
\theta(t) = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{s\,\Phi\,t}{n_0}\right)
$$ {#eq-langmuir}

The simulation below evaluates @eq-flux and @eq-langmuir for TMA (M = 72.09 g mol^−1^) and scales the GPC by the coverage.

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.3: Estimating the saturating dose]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof P_mTorr = Inputs.range([0.5, 100], {value: 10, step: 0.5, label: "Partial pressure (mTorr)"})
viewof T_C = Inputs.range([50, 350], {value: 200, step: 5, label: "Temperature (°C)"})
viewof logS = Inputs.range([-5, -1], {value: -3, step: 0.1, label: "log₁₀ sticking probability, s"})
viewof n0_e14 = Inputs.range([1, 10], {value: 4, step: 0.5, label: "Reactive sites (10¹⁴ cm⁻²)"})
viewof gpcSat = Inputs.range([0.2, 2], {value: 1.1, step: 0.05, label: "Saturated GPC (Å)"})
viewof tPulse = Inputs.range([0.001, 1], {value: 0.3, step: 0.001, label: "Pulse time (s)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
satModel = {
  const kB = 1.380649e-23, NA = 6.02214076e23, M = 72.09e-3;   // TMA
  const p = P_mTorr * 0.133322;                                  // Pa
  const m = M / NA;                                              // kg
  const T = T_C + 273.15;
  const flux = p / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI * m * kB * T) / 1e4;    // cm^-2 s^-1
  const k = Math.pow(10, logS) * flux / (n0_e14 * 1e14);         // s^-1
  const t99 = Math.log(100) / k;
  const tMax = Math.max(3 * t99, 1.2 * tPulse);
  const pts = d3.range(0, 201).map(i => {
    const t = tMax * i / 200;
    return {t, gpc: gpcSat * (1 - Math.exp(-k * t))};
  });
  const theta = 1 - Math.exp(-k * tPulse);
  return {flux, k, t99, pts, theta, exposureL: P_mTorr * 1e-3 * tPulse / 1e-6,
          exposure99L: P_mTorr * 1e-3 * t99 / 1e-6};
}

Plot.plot({
  height: 340, marginLeft: 65, marginBottom: 50, marginTop: 30,
  x: {label: "Pulse time (s) →"},
  y: {label: "↑ GPC (Å)", domain: [0, gpcSat * 1.1], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([gpcSat], {stroke: "#8C8C8C", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(satModel.pts, {x: "t", y: "gpc", stroke: "#000000", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([satModel.t99], {stroke: "#4D4D4D", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),
    Plot.dot([{t: tPulse, gpc: gpcSat * satModel.theta}], {x: "t", y: "gpc", r: 6, fill: "#E91C24"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Flux: **${satModel.flux.toExponential(2)} cm⁻² s⁻¹** · Coverage at this pulse: **${(100 * satModel.theta).toFixed(1)} %** · Exposure: **${satModel.exposureL.toFixed(0)} L**

Pulse needed for 99 % coverage (dotted line): **${satModel.t99 < 1 ? (1000 * satModel.t99).toFixed(1) + " ms" : satModel.t99.toFixed(2) + " s"}** (≈ ${satModel.exposure99L.toExponential(1)} L)`
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions:** planar substrate; ideal-gas flux at the substrate temperature; constant precursor partial pressure during the pulse; first-order Langmuir adsorption with constant $s$; GPC proportional to coverage of this half-reaction only (the other half-reaction is assumed saturated); no CVD or decomposition contribution. 1 L (Langmuir) = 10^−6^ Torr s.
:::
:::

Things to try:

- Change *s* by one decade and watch the saturation time change by a decade as well. Reported sticking probabilities vary over orders of magnitude, so a "saturating dose" taken from someone else's reactor is only a starting point.
- Notice that the model contains **no** temperature dependence of *s*. In real systems *s* is often thermally activated, which couples dose requirements to the temperature window (@sec-ald-window).

**High aspect ratio structures.** In a trench or pore, molecules must diffuse in, mostly in the Knudsen regime, while being consumed on the walls. The exposure needed for conformal coverage therefore grows steeply with aspect ratio: for large aspect ratios it scales roughly with the aspect ratio squared [@Gordon2003]. Doses that saturate a planar witness wafer can badly undercoat a high-aspect-ratio sample.

### Steric crowding: why one cycle is not one monolayer {#sec-steric}

A saturated TMA half-cycle does not deposit a monolayer of Al~2~O~3~. Each chemisorbed fragment keeps one or two methyl groups, and these take up much more room on the surface than a bare aluminum atom would [@Barry2022]. The methyls cover neighbouring –OH groups so that no further TMA molecule can reach them. The half-reaction saturates when every remaining –OH is either consumed or shielded. That point comes long before the surface holds a full layer of aluminum. In other words, a saturated layer of chemisorbed precursor is not a monolayer of the target film [@Barry2022; @Puurunen2005].

There are two ways the coverage can be limited:

- **Site-limited.** If –OH groups are sparse, TMA can reach all of them. The amount of Al per cycle is then set by the hydroxyl density.
- **Sterically limited.** If –OH groups are dense, the ligands of the first fragments to land block the rest. The amount of Al per cycle is then set by the size of the fragments, not by the number of sites.

Which regime applies depends on the precursor and the temperature, because the hydroxyl density falls as the surface dehydroxylates at higher temperature [@Puurunen2005].

The simulation below drops TMA molecules at random onto a 10 nm × 10 nm patch of hydroxylated surface. Each molecule that lands on a free, unshielded –OH chemisorbs, either as a dimethyl species (one –OH) or, if a second free –OH is close by, as a monomethyl species (two –OH). Set the methyl diameter to zero to switch off steric hindrance and see the site-limited case.

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.4: Steric crowding during the TMA half-cycle]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ohDens = Inputs.range([2, 12], {value: 8, step: 0.5, label: "–OH density (nm⁻²)"})
viewof meD = Inputs.range([0, 4.5], {value: 3.5, step: 0.1, label: "Methyl group diameter (Å)"})
viewof pBi = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.4, step: 0.05, label: "Probability of reacting with two –OH"})
viewof expo = Inputs.range([0, 6], {value: 6, step: 0.05, label: "TMA exposure (arrivals per –OH)"})
viewof reseed = Inputs.button("New random surface")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
steric = {
  reseed;                                            // re-run on button press
  const L = 100;                                     // patch size, Å
  let seed = (Math.random() * 2 ** 32) >>> 0;
  const rnd = () => {                                // mulberry32
    seed |= 0; seed = (seed + 0x6D2B79F5) | 0;
    let t = Math.imul(seed ^ (seed >>> 15), 1 | seed);
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
  const N = Math.round(ohDens * L * L / 100);
  const sites = d3.range(N).map(() => ({x: rnd() * L, y: rnd() * L, used: false}));
  const wrap = v => v - L * Math.round(v / L);
  const dist = (a, b) => Math.hypot(wrap(a.x - b.x), wrap(a.y - b.y));
  // neighbour lists for bifunctional reaction (second –OH within 3.5 Å)
  const nb = sites.map((s, i) => sites.map((t, j) => j).filter(j => j !== i && dist(s, sites[j]) < 3.5));
  const dDi = meD * Math.SQRT2, dMono = meD;         // footprint diameters
  const frags = [];
  const fits = (c, d) => frags.every(f => dist(c, f) >= (d + f.d) / 2);
  const total = Math.round(6 * N), curve = [{e: 0, al: 0}];
  for (let k = 1; k <= total; k++) {
    const i = Math.floor(rnd() * N), s = sites[i];
    if (!s.used) {
      let placed = false;
      if (rnd() < pBi) {
        const free = nb[i].filter(j => !sites[j].used);
        if (free.length) {
          const j = free.reduce((a, b) => dist(s, sites[a]) < dist(s, sites[b]) ? a : b);
          const t = sites[j];
          const c = {x: (s.x + wrap(t.x - s.x) / 2 + L) % L, y: (s.y + wrap(t.y - s.y) / 2 + L) % L};
          if (fits(c, dMono)) {
            s.used = t.used = true;
            frags.push({...c, d: dMono, me: 1, k, a: s, b: t});
            placed = true;
          }
        }
      }
      if (!placed && fits(s, dDi)) { s.used = true; frags.push({x: s.x, y: s.y, d: dDi, me: 2, k, a: s}); }
    }
    if (k % Math.max(1, Math.round(N / 20)) === 0) curve.push({e: k / N, al: frags.length});
  }
  return {L, N, sites, frags, curve};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
stericNow = {
  const kMax = expo * steric.N;
  const frags = steric.frags.filter(f => f.k <= kMax);
  const used = new Set(frags.flatMap(f => f.me === 1 ? [f.a, f.b] : [f.a]));
  const area = steric.L * steric.L / 100;            // nm²
  const al = frags.length / area;                    // Al nm⁻²
  const me = frags.reduce((s, f) => s + f.me, 0) / area;
  const vAl = 101.96 / (2 * 3.0 * 6.02214e23) * 1e24;// Å³ per Al at 3.0 g cm⁻³
  const gpc = al / 100 * vAl;                        // Å
  const ml = Math.cbrt(vAl);                         // Å, one "layer" of Al2O3
  return {frags, used, al, me, gpc, ml, ohUsed: used.size / steric.N,
          nMono: frags.filter(f => f.me === 1).length, nDi: frags.filter(f => f.me === 2).length};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Al adsorbed: **${stericNow.al.toFixed(2)} nm⁻²** (${stericNow.nDi} dimethyl, ${stericNow.nMono} monomethyl) · –OH consumed: **${(100 * stericNow.ohUsed).toFixed(0)} %** · CH₃ left for the water step: **${stericNow.me.toFixed(2)} nm⁻²**

```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** Random sequential adsorption: TMA arrives at random –OH sites, sticks irreversibly where it lands, and never moves. Each fragment's footprint is a disc: a dimethyl species covers the area of two methyl groups, a monomethyl species the area of one. A molecule chemisorbs only if its footprint does not overlap an existing one. A monomethyl species forms only when a second free –OH lies within 3.5 Å. –OH groups are placed at random, and edges wrap around. TMA reaction with Al–O bridges is left out. The GPC conversion assumes each adsorbed Al ends up in Al~2~O~3~ of density 3.0 g cm^−3^.

**Where it fails.** With realistic settings the model gives 0.6–0.9 Å, below the measured ~1.1 Å. Random, irreversible adsorption is the least efficient way to pack a surface, real fragments can rearrange, and the omitted reaction with Al–O bridges adds Al without consuming –OH. Use the model for trends (how coverage responds to –OH density and ligand size), not for absolute numbers.
:::
:::

#### What is "typical" coverage for TMA/H~2~O?

A useful way to express coverage is to compare the GPC with the thickness of one "layer" of the film. For Al~2~O~3~ with a density of about 3.0 g cm^−3^, the volume per Al atom is

$$
V_\text{Al} = \frac{M_{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3}}{2\,\rho\,N_\text{A}} = \frac{101.96\ \text{g mol}^{-1}}{2 \times 3.0\ \text{g cm}^{-3} \times 6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}} \approx 28\ \text{Å}^3
$$ {#eq-val}

The cube root of this volume, about 3 Å, is a reasonable estimate of the thickness of one layer; @Barry2022 quotes about 2.9 Å. A typical TMA/H~2~O GPC of 1.1 Å therefore corresponds to:

- **About 30–40 % of a monolayer** of Al~2~O~3~ per cycle, depending on temperature and nucleation-site density [@Barry2022].
- **About 4 Al atoms per nm^2^ per cycle** (1.1 Å ÷ 28 Å^3^ ≈ 0.039 Å^−2^), compared with roughly 11 nm^−2^ for a complete layer.

So it takes about three cycles to deposit the equivalent of one layer of aluminum oxide. After the TMA pulse, the surface is a mixture of fragments that have lost one methyl group and fragments that have lost two [@Barry2022]. Their ratio sets how many methyls go on to the water step, and both the ratio and the –OH density shift with temperature. This is why the GPC of TMA/H~2~O changes with deposition temperature even though each half-reaction is self-limiting [@Puurunen2005].

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
### Saturation is not a monolayer
"Saturated" means the surface will take up no more precursor. It does not mean the surface is covered with a full layer of metal atoms. For almost every ALD process, a saturated half-cycle deposits a fraction of a monolayer of the final film.
:::

The same argument resolves a puzzle about substrates. At room temperature, silica carries 4–5 hydroxyls per nm^2^ and alumina about 15, so alumina might be expected to grow much faster. In practice both oxides have a GPC of about 1 Å from TMA, and the TMA half-reaction plateaus at 30–40 % of a monolayer [@Barry2022]. When the sites are dense, the size of the adsorbed fragments, not the number of sites, sets the GPC. Chemisorption can also follow more than one path (loss of one or two methane molecules per TMA), and each path leaves a fragment with a different footprint. Simple geometric models of these footprints are often enough to explain a low GPC [@Barry2022].

### Process windows {#sec-process-windows}

Every atomic layer process has a range of conditions in which each step is self-limiting. For thermal ALD the variable is temperature, and the range is called the ALD window.

#### The ALD window and its limits {#sec-ald-window}

GPC is commonly plotted against temperature, and the range over which it is approximately constant is called the **ALD window**. On either side, growth departs from the ideal for different reasons:

| Region | GPC trend | Typical cause |
|---|---|---|
| Low *T*, high GPC | ↑ | Precursor or co-reactant condensation; physisorbed water not removed by the purge |
| Low *T*, low GPC | ↓ | Insufficient thermal energy; the reaction is too slow to saturate in the pulse time |
| High *T*, high GPC | ↑ | Precursor decomposition, which adds a CVD-like, non-self-limiting component |
| High *T*, low GPC | ↓ | Desorption of chemisorbed species, or loss of reactive sites (e.g. dehydroxylation) |

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.5: A qualitative ALD window]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof Tlow = Inputs.range([50, 250], {value: 140, step: 5, label: "Lower edge (°C)"})
viewof Thigh = Inputs.range([150, 450], {value: 300, step: 5, label: "Upper edge (°C)"})
viewof slope = Inputs.range([-0.4, 0.4], {value: 0, step: 0.02, label: "GPC slope inside window (Å per 100 °C)"})
viewof lowMode = Inputs.radio(["Condensation", "Insufficient reactivity"], {value: "Insufficient reactivity", label: "Below the window"})
viewof highMode = Inputs.radio(["Decomposition", "Desorption / site loss"], {value: "Decomposition", label: "Above the window"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
windowPts = {
  const g0 = 1.0;
  const hi = Math.max(Thigh, Tlow + 20);
  const mid = (Tlow + hi) / 2;
  const inside = T => g0 + slope * (T - mid) / 100;
  const g = T => {
    if (T < Tlow) {
      const d = Tlow - T;
      return lowMode === "Condensation" ? inside(Tlow) * (1 + 1.5 * (1 - Math.exp(-d / 40)))
                                        : inside(Tlow) * Math.exp(-d / 35);
    }
    if (T > hi) {
      const d = T - hi;
      return highMode === "Decomposition" ? inside(hi) * Math.exp(d / 60)
                                          : inside(hi) * Math.exp(-d / 70);
    }
    return inside(T);
  };
  return {hi, pts: d3.range(25, 501, 2).map(T => ({T, gpc: Math.max(0, g(T))}))};
}

Plot.plot({
  height: 340, marginLeft: 65, marginBottom: 50, marginTop: 30,
  x: {label: "Deposition temperature (°C) →", domain: [25, 500]},
  y: {label: "↑ GPC (relative)", domain: [0, 3], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX([{x1: Tlow, x2: windowPts.hi}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: 0, y2: 3, fill: "#8C8C8C", fillOpacity: 0.15}),
    Plot.text([{x: (Tlow + windowPts.hi) / 2, y: 2.8, label: "\"window\""}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "label", fill: "#4D4D4D"}),
    Plot.line(windowPts.pts, {x: "T", y: "gpc", stroke: "#000000", strokeWidth: 2, clip: true})
  ]
})
```

::: {.assumptions}
**This is a schematic, not a physical model.** The functional forms outside the window are chosen only to show the direction of each effect. Use it to reason about which mechanism could explain a data set, not to fit data.
:::
:::

**A critical view of the window.** The flat plateau is a teaching idealization, and it causes two common errors:

1. *Self-limiting is not the same as temperature-independent.* For TMA/H~2~O, the GPC falls steadily with temperature over the whole useful range because the surface hydroxyl density decreases [@Puurunen2005]. The process is still self-limiting at each temperature. Set the slope slider to a negative value to see what this looks like.
2. *A plateau does not prove self-limitation.* An approximately constant GPC over some range can arise from competing effects, for example slow decomposition offset by site loss. Only dose and purge series at each temperature establish ALD behaviour.

Film properties such as crystallinity, density and impurity content also change across the "window". Crystallization onset, for example, depends on the material and the temperature, so a constant GPC does not mean a constant film [@Miikkulainen2013].

A self-limiting process can even have more than one plateau. InN grown from trimethylindium and an NH~3~ plasma shows a GPC plateau of 0.4 Å around 220 °C and a second plateau of 1.2 Å around 300 °C, and saturation curves show self-limiting growth at both temperatures [@Barry2022]. Whether the jump comes from a change in the density of nucleation sites, a shift in the balance between k~a~ and k~d~, or a gas-phase reaction that starts at higher temperature cannot be decided from the GPC data alone. Further experiments are needed: a GPC plateau tells you where to look, not what is happening.

#### Windows in the other processes

The same idea carries over, with different variables:

- **ALE** has its own window. In directional (plasma) ALE, the variable is ion energy: there is a range above the energy needed to remove the modified layer and below the energy that sputters the unmodified material, in which the etch per cycle (EPC) is constant [@Kanarik2015]. Thermal ALE has temperature windows, because its ligand-exchange step often works only above a threshold temperature. Both are treated in the ALE chapter (in preparation).
- **MLD** windows are usually narrower than ALD windows, because organic precursors condense at low temperature and decompose at moderate temperature.
- **ASD** adds a window in *cycles*: selectivity holds only until enough nuclei form on the non-growth surface (@sec-nucleation-energetics).

## Ligands {#sec-ligands}

[Applies to: ALD · MLD · ALE (ligand exchange) · ASD (inhibitors)]{.applies}

Ligands are not only an ALD topic. In thermal ALE, the removal step is a ligand-exchange reaction that turns the surface into a volatile metal complex. In ASD, many small-molecule inhibitors are ligands chosen to bind one surface and not another. The bonding ideas below apply to all of them.

### What a ligand has to do

In metal-organic chemistry, a ligand is a group bonded directly to a metal centre, through one atom or several [@Barry2022]. In an ALD precursor, the ligands carry the metal (the "payload" atom) into the reactor, and are then removed by surface chemistry. That gives them two jobs that pull in opposite directions:

- The metal–ligand bonds must be **strong enough** to survive vaporization, delivery and the hot reactor without breaking.
- They must also be **easy enough to remove** in the half-reactions, so that the ligand leaves cleanly and does not stay in the film as an impurity [@Barry2022].

Put another way, a good precursor has to balance volatility, thermal stability and reactivity, and do all three while reacting self-limitingly. Compounds that strike this balance are uncommon, and for many metals none are known yet. Discovering and implementing a new ligand is one of the main contributions a chemist can make to ALD [@Barry2022].

### Ligand bonding {#sec-ligand-bonding}

#### L and X ligands

A ligand is a Lewis base: it donates electron density into an empty orbital on the metal, which acts as a Lewis acid [@Barry2022]. For bookkeeping, ligands fall into two types:

- **L ligands** are neutral donors that supply both electrons of the bond. Examples: CO, NH~3~, phosphines, ethers, N-heterocyclic carbenes.
- **X ligands** are formally anionic. In the covalent picture, the metal and the ligand each contribute one electron to the bond. Examples: CH~3~^−^, Cl^−^, NR~2~^−^, OR^−^.

This is a model for counting electrons, but it has a practical consequence for ALD. When an **L** ligand dissociates, both fragments are neutral, and the metal-containing fragment can survive in the gas phase even if it is less stable. When an **X** ligand dissociates heterolytically, it leaves a cation, which does not survive in the gas phase under reasonable conditions. So L ligands can complicate the gas-phase chemistry of a precursor much more than X ligands do [@Barry2022].

##### Why is methyl a ligand?

Consider trimethylaluminum. Each methyl is an X ligand whose conjugate acid is methane. Deprotonating methane (CH~4~ → CH~3~^−^ + H^+^) costs about 440 kJ mol^−1^, which is not very different from the H–Cl bond strength (428 kJ mol^−1^) [@Barry2022]. Yet HCl is a strong acid and methane is not. The difference is electronegativity, not bond strength: carbon (2.55) and hydrogen (2.20) share the bonding pair almost evenly, while chlorine (3.16) pulls it towards itself and releases H^+^ easily [@Barry2022]. Bond polarity, not just bond strength, is what decides how a bond breaks. We use this idea again below.

##### Back-bonding

Carbon monoxide is the classic L ligand. It donates its lone pair to the metal and, at the same time, accepts electron density from filled metal d orbitals into its empty π\* orbitals. This **back-bonding** makes the M–CO bond stronger than a simple dative bond, at the cost of weakening the C≡O bond [@Barry2022]. Isonitriles (R–NC) behave similarly. Metal carbonyls are a mature area of organometallic chemistry but are still under-represented in ALD [@Barry2022].

The diagram below compares the three bonding situations in this section. Choose a ligand type to see how it bonds to the metal.

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.6: σ donation and π back-bonding]{.sim-title}


```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const red = "#E91C24", dark = "#4D4D4D", grey = "#8C8C8C", light = "#EDEDED";
  const isCO = bondMode.startsWith("CO"), isX = bondMode.startsWith("X");
  const x = isCO ? 0.6 : 0;                         // fixed, schematic amount of back-donation
  const M = [220, 175], D = isCO ? [455, 175] : [470, 175], O = [555, 175];
  const e = (cx, cy) => `<circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="4.5" fill="#000"/>`;
  const atom = ([cx, cy], lab, fill, r = 22) =>
    `<circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${r}" fill="${fill}" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.2"/>
     <text x="${cx}" y="${cy + 6}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="17" font-weight="600" fill="${fill === "#FFFFFF" ? "#000" : "#fff"}">${lab}</text>`;
  const arrow = (d, col, w, lab, lx, ly) =>
    `<path d="${d}" fill="none" stroke="${col}" stroke-width="${w}" marker-end="url(#bbArr)" style="color:${col}"/>
     <text x="${lx}" y="${ly}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="600" fill="${col}">${lab}</text>`;
  let g = "";

  // π system for CO: metal d orbital (four lobes) and CO π* (large on C, small on O)
  if (isCO) {
    const op = 0.15 + 0.75 * x;
    [[1, -1, dark], [-1, 1, dark], [1, 1, "#FFFFFF"], [-1, -1, "#FFFFFF"]].forEach(([sx, sy, f]) => {
      g += `<ellipse cx="${M[0] + 30 * sx}" cy="${M[1] + 30 * sy}" rx="30" ry="13" transform="rotate(${sx * sy > 0 ? 45 : -45} ${M[0] + 30 * sx} ${M[1] + 30 * sy})" fill="${f}" fill-opacity="0.8" stroke="#000" stroke-width="0.8"/>`;
    });
    g += e(M[0] + 36, M[1] - 36) + e(M[0] + 26, M[1] - 26);
    g += `<ellipse cx="${D[0]}" cy="${D[1] - 42}" rx="16" ry="32" fill="${red}" fill-opacity="${op}" stroke="${red}" stroke-width="1"/>
          <ellipse cx="${D[0]}" cy="${D[1] + 42}" rx="16" ry="32" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="${red}" stroke-width="1"/>
          <ellipse cx="${O[0]}" cy="${O[1] - 30}" rx="11" ry="20" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="${red}" stroke-width="1"/>
          <ellipse cx="${O[0]}" cy="${O[1] + 30}" rx="11" ry="20" fill="${red}" fill-opacity="${op}" stroke="${red}" stroke-width="1"/>
          <text x="${(D[0] + O[0]) / 2 + 4}" y="${D[1] - 82}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="${red}">CO π* (empty)</text>
          <text x="${M[0]}" y="${M[1] - 78}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="${dark}">filled metal d orbital</text>`;
    g += arrow(`M${M[0] + 50},${M[1] - 58} Q${(M[0] + D[0]) / 2},${M[1] - 120} ${D[0] - 20},${D[1] - 60}`, dark, 1.5 + 4 * x,
      "π back-donation", (M[0] + D[0]) / 2, M[1] - 100);
  }

  // σ system: metal acceptor lobe and ligand donor lobe on the M–D axis
  const metalLobe = `<ellipse cx="${M[0] + 62}" cy="${M[1]}" rx="40" ry="20" fill="${isX ? light : "#FFFFFF"}" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="${isX ? "" : "4,3"}"/>`;
  const ligLobe = `<ellipse cx="${D[0] - 66}" cy="${D[1]}" rx="44" ry="22" fill="${red}" fill-opacity="0.35" stroke="${red}" stroke-width="1"/>`;
  g += metalLobe + ligLobe;
  if (isX) g += e(M[0] + 62, M[1]) + e(D[0] - 66, D[1]);
  else g += e(D[0] - 74, D[1]) + e(D[0] - 58, D[1]);
  const sigmaLab = isX ? "1 e⁻ from M + 1 e⁻ from X" : "σ donation: 2 e⁻ from ligand";
  const ay = M[1] + (isCO ? 105 : 60);
  if (isX) {
    // shared pair: bracket, no arrow
    g += `<path d="M${M[0] + 30},${ay - 12} V${ay} H${D[0] - 30} V${ay - 12}" fill="none" stroke="${red}" stroke-width="2"/>
          <text x="${(M[0] + D[0]) / 2}" y="${ay + 22}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="600" fill="${red}">${sigmaLab}</text>`;
  } else {
    g += arrow(`M${D[0] - 50},${ay} L${M[0] + 50},${ay}`, red, 2.5, sigmaLab, (M[0] + D[0]) / 2, ay + 23);
  }

  // bonds and atoms
  if (isCO) {
    [-6, 0, 6].forEach((dy, i) => {
      const op = i === 0 ? Math.max(0.12, 1 - x) : 1;
      g += `<line x1="${D[0]}" y1="${D[1] + dy}" x2="${O[0]}" y2="${O[1] + dy}" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2" stroke-opacity="${op}"/>`;
    });
  }
  g += atom(M, "M", dark);
  g += atom(D, isCO ? "C" : isX ? "X" : "L", isCO ? "#000000" : red);
  if (isCO) g += atom(O, "O", red, 19);

  const svg = `<svg viewBox="${isCO ? "0 0 680 330" : "0 120 680 150"}" width="100%" style="max-width:720px" role="img" aria-label="Orbital diagram: ${bondMode}">
    <defs><marker id="bbArr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs>
    ${g}</svg>`;

  const note = isCO
    ? `CO donates its lone pair to the metal (σ), and the metal pushes electron density from a filled d orbital back into CO's empty π* orbital. Back-donation strengthens the metal–carbon bond to more than a single bond and weakens C≡O, because the electrons go into an antibonding orbital of CO. This is why metal carbonyls show a lower C–O stretching frequency than free CO (2143 cm⁻¹).`
    : isX
    ? `The metal and the ligand each supply one electron. Heterolytic cleavage gives X⁻ and a metal <b>cation</b>, which does not survive in the gas phase under reasonable conditions.`
    : `The ligand supplies both electrons; the metal orbital is empty. Losing L leaves a <b>neutral</b> metal fragment that can survive in the gas phase, which is why L ligands can complicate precursor chemistry.`;
  return html`<div>${html([svg])}<div class="map-card" style="margin-top:0.5rem">${html([note])}</div></div>`;
}
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** A cartoon, not a calculation: one metal d orbital and one of the two degenerate CO π\* orbitals are shown, and lobe sizes and the amount of back-donation drawn are schematic. Filled lobes have one phase and open lobes the other. π back-donation needs a filled metal d orbital whose lobe has the same phase as the π\* lobe on carbon it overlaps.
:::
:::


#### Bond polarity: where will the bond break?

The metals of the first transition series (Sc to Zn) have Pauling electronegativities between about 1.36 and 1.91, while N is 3.04 and O is 3.44. Metal–N and metal–O bonds are therefore strongly polarized towards the ligand [@Barry2022]. Pauling related the ionic character of a bond to the electronegativity difference Δχ between the two atoms:

$$
\%\,\text{ionicity} = -4.94\,(\Delta\chi)^3 + 23.0\,(\Delta\chi)^2 + 5.75\,\Delta\chi - 1.34
$$ {#eq-ionicity}

Combining ionicity with bond enthalpy gives a first prediction of precursor behaviour [@Barry2022]:

- A **strong but highly ionic** bond tends to survive heating, but breaks cleanly at the metal under chemical attack. The ligand leaves intact.
- A **weaker, more covalent** bond is more likely to fail thermally, and to fail somewhere other than the metal–ligand bond. Fragments of the ligand can then stay behind as impurities.

Use the explorer below to compare donor atoms for a chosen metal.

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.7: Metal–ligand bond ionicity]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
chiMetal = new Map([
  ["Al", 1.61], ["Ga", 1.81], ["Si", 1.90], ["Sn", 1.96],
  ["Sc", 1.36], ["Y", 1.22], ["La", 1.10],
  ["Ti", 1.54], ["Zr", 1.33], ["Hf", 1.30],
  ["V", 1.63], ["Cr", 1.66], ["Mn", 1.55], ["Fe", 1.83], ["Co", 1.88], ["Ni", 1.91], ["Cu", 1.90], ["Zn", 1.65],
  ["Ru", 2.20], ["Pt", 2.28]
])
chiDonor = [
  {el: "H", chi: 2.20, ligand: "hydride"},
  {el: "C", chi: 2.55, ligand: "alkyl, Cp"},
  {el: "S", chi: 2.58, ligand: "thiolate"},
  {el: "I", chi: 2.66, ligand: "iodide"},
  {el: "Br", chi: 2.96, ligand: "bromide"},
  {el: "N", chi: 3.04, ligand: "amide, amidinate"},
  {el: "Cl", chi: 3.16, ligand: "chloride"},
  {el: "O", chi: 3.44, ligand: "alkoxide, β-diketonate"},
  {el: "F", chi: 3.98, ligand: "fluoride"}
]
ionicity = d => Math.max(0, Math.min(100, -4.94 * d ** 3 + 23.0 * d ** 2 + 5.75 * d - 1.34))
viewof metal = Inputs.select([...chiMetal.keys()], {value: "Sc", label: "Metal"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bonds = chiDonor.map(d => {
  const dchi = Math.abs(d.chi - chiMetal.get(metal));
  return {...d, bond: `${metal}–${d.el}`, dchi, ion: ionicity(dchi)};
})

Plot.plot({
  height: 340, marginLeft: 60, marginBottom: 50, marginTop: 30,
  x: {label: "Electronegativity difference, Δχ →", domain: [0, 3]},
  y: {label: "↑ Ionic character (%)", domain: [0, 100], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(d3.range(0, 3.001, 0.02).map(x => ({x, y: ionicity(x)})), {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#8C8C8C", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.dot(bonds, {x: "dchi", y: "ion", r: 6, fill: d => d.el === "N" || d.el === "O" ? "#E91C24" : "#000000",
      channels: {Bond: "bond", "Typical ligand": "ligand"}, tip: {format: {x: ".2f", y: ".0f", fill: false}}}),
    // S, Br and I are unlabelled to avoid overlap; hover or see the table
    Plot.text(bonds.filter(b => ["H", "C", "N", "O", "Cl", "F"].includes(b.el)), {x: "dchi", y: "ion", text: "bond", dy: -12, fontSize: 12})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Inputs.table(bonds.map(b => ({Bond: b.bond, "Typical ligand": b.ligand, "Δχ": b.dchi, "Ionic (%)": b.ion})),
  {sort: "Ionic (%)", reverse: true, rows: 10,
   format: {"Δχ": x => x.toFixed(2), "Ionic (%)": x => x.toFixed(0)}})
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** Pauling electronegativities; @eq-ionicity applied to the absolute value of Δχ and capped at 0–100 %. Ionicity says nothing on its own about bond *strength*, which must come from bond enthalpies. Real precursors also depend on the rest of the molecule: the other ligands, oxidation state, sterics and the co-reactant.
:::
:::

##### Two worked comparisons

**Sc–O versus Sc–N.** Scandium has the lowest electronegativity of the first-row transition metals, so it is the most mismatched with both N and O. The Sc–O bond is about 66 % ionic and strong (682 kJ mol^−1^); Sc–N is about 50 % ionic and weaker (470 kJ mol^−1^). So Sc(thd)~3~, with Sc–O bonds, should hold on to its ligands at intermediate temperatures but cleave at the Sc–O bond when it reacts. Sc(iPrAMD)~3~, with Sc–N bonds, should decompose at lower temperatures, and more likely at a bond other than Sc–N, which can leave nitrogen in the film [@Barry2022].

**AlMe~3~ versus AlCl~3~.** Both are homoleptic, three-coordinate Al(III) precursors for Al~2~O~3~ [@Barry2022].

| | AlMe~3~ (TMA) | AlCl~3~ |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Al–X bond enthalpy | 268 kJ mol^−1^ | 502 kJ mol^−1^ |
| Ionic character | ~20 % | ~44 % |
| Deposition range (with H~2~O or alcohols) | Room temperature to ~300 °C (TMA decomposes above this) | 250–500 °C |
| Typical impurities | Up to ~30 % C at low temperature; 3–5 % near 250 °C | Cl < 2 % (often undetectable), C < 2 % |
| By-product | CH~4~ | HCl (corrosive) |

: TMA and AlCl~3~ compared [@Barry2022]. {#tbl-tma-alcl3}

The weaker, more covalent Al–C bond is more likely to leave an impurity at low temperature than the stronger, more ionic Al–Cl bond. TMA still wins in most labs because it reacts at much lower temperatures and avoids corrosive HCl. The trade-off depends on the application: its thermal budget, its tolerance for impurities, and how robust the process must be [@Barry2022].

#### The chelate effect {#sec-chelate}

A **chelating** ligand binds the metal through two or more atoms. Amidinates and β-diketonates are common examples in ALD. Chelates are more stable than comparable monodentate ligands for two reasons [@Barry2022]:

- **Enthalpy.** Many chelates are resonance-stabilized: the negative charge is shared over both donor atoms, so neither bond is purely L or purely X.
- **Entropy.** Losing a chelating ligand releases one particle, M(L~2~)~n~ ⇌ M(L~2~)~n−1~ + L~2~. Losing the equivalent two monodentate ligands releases two, ML~2n~ ⇌ ML~2n−2~ + 2 L. There is less entropic drive to lose the chelate.

The effect is easiest to measure in solution. Replacing two waters on Cu(H~2~O)~6~^2+^ with two NH~3~ ligands, or with one ethylenediamine (en, H~2~N–CH~2~CH~2~–NH~2~), has a similar enthalpy change, but very different entropy changes [@Barry2022]:

| Reaction | ΔH (kJ mol^−1^) | ΔS (J K^−1^ mol^−1^) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Cu(H~2~O)~6~^2+^ + 2 NH~3~ → Cu(H~2~O)~4~(NH~3~)~2~^2+^ + 2 H~2~O | −46 | −8.4 |
| Cu(H~2~O)~6~^2+^ + en → Cu(H~2~O)~4~(en)^2+^ + 2 H~2~O | −54 | +23 |

: Thermodynamics of the chelate effect for Cu^2+^ [@Barry2022]. {#tbl-chelate}

Because the entropy term is multiplied by temperature in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, the chelate advantage grows as the temperature rises, which is relevant to ALD reactors running at 400–600 K.

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.8: The chelate effect and temperature]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof T_K = Inputs.range([250, 700], {value: 300, step: 5, label: "Temperature (K)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
chel = {
  const rx = [
    {name: "2 NH₃ (monodentate)", dH: -46, dS: -8.4},
    {name: "en (chelate)", dH: -54, dS: 23}
  ];
  const G = (r, T) => r.dH - T * r.dS / 1000;
  const lines = rx.flatMap(r => d3.range(250, 701, 10).map(T => ({name: r.name, T, G: G(r, T)})));
  const now = rx.map(r => ({name: r.name, T: T_K, G: G(r, T_K)}));
  return {lines, now};
}

Plot.plot({
  height: 320, marginLeft: 65, marginBottom: 50, marginTop: 20,
  x: {label: "Temperature (K) →", domain: [250, 700]},
  y: {label: "↑ ΔG (kJ mol⁻¹)", grid: true},
  color: {domain: ["2 NH₃ (monodentate)", "en (chelate)"], range: ["#8C8C8C", "#E91C24"], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([T_K], {stroke: "#4D4D4D", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),
    Plot.line(chel.lines, {x: "T", y: "G", stroke: "name", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(chel.now, {x: "T", y: "G", fill: "name", r: 6})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`At **${T_K} K** (${(T_K - 273.15).toFixed(0)} °C): ΔG(2 NH₃) = **${chel.now[0].G.toFixed(1)} kJ mol⁻¹**, ΔG(en) = **${chel.now[1].G.toFixed(1)} kJ mol⁻¹**. The chelate is favoured by **${(chel.now[0].G - chel.now[1].G).toFixed(1)} kJ mol⁻¹**.`
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** ΔH and ΔS are aqueous values near room temperature, held constant over the whole range. Extrapolating them to 700 K, and from solution to the gas phase or a surface, is for illustration only: the point is the trend with temperature, not the numbers.
:::
:::

##### Chelates and saturation

Because chelating ligands are less likely to dissociate, they can also protect the payload atom once it is on the surface. A chelate that stays attached after chemisorption adds steric bulk that blocks further adsorption, which helps the half-reaction self-limit (@sec-steric). The metal–ligand bond then has to be tuned so the ligand stays on during the precursor pulse but is removed completely in the next one. Ligands that are retained are a major source of film impurities, so the identity of the atom bonded to the metal deserves careful thought [@Barry2022].

#### Tunable ligand families {#sec-tunable-families}

Ligands are often chosen for how easily their frameworks can be modified. A good example is the family of β-diketonates, β-ketoiminates and β-diiminates [@Barry2022]. All are deprotonated at the central carbon of the bridge, and the negative charge is delocalized over the two donor atoms E (O or N). The β-diketonate is made by condensing a ketone with an acid chloride, and stepwise reaction with primary amines replaces O donors with N [@Barry2022]. Each R group comes from a different reagent, so the symmetry and bulk of the ligand are easy to change.

Switching O to N changes several things at once [@Barry2022]:

- **Bond strength.** A different donor atom gives a different metal–ligand bond: stronger bonds improve thermal stability, weaker ones make the ligand easier to remove in the next pulse.
- **Impurities.** A precursor for a nitride film should bond through N, because O would be an impurity.
- **Sterics close to the metal.** On N, the R groups sit right next to the metal. Small groups (CH~3~) let the ligand approach closely and bond strongly; bulky groups (C(CH~3~)~3~) push it away and weaken the bond. Two N donors (β-diiminate) weaken the bonding more than one (β-ketoiminate).

#### Bridging ligands: why TMA is a dimer

Both AlCl~3~ and AlMe~3~ are dimers under standard conditions, Al~2~Cl~6~ and Al~2~Me~6~, but the bridges are different [@Barry2022]:

- Each bridging **chloride** has lone pairs to spare and uses two electron pairs to bind both Al atoms: a **3-centre, 4-electron** (3c4e) bond.
- Each bridging **methyl** has only one electron pair, shared across both Al atoms: a **3-centre, 2-electron** (3c2e) bond, which is inherently weaker.

In the gas phase, both precursors are in equilibrium between monomer and dimer, and the surface reaction generally proceeds through the monomer [@Barry2022]. Methyl is also smaller than chloride, so methyl fragments can pack more densely on the surface, giving a higher GPC [@Barry2022]. This is the steric-crowding argument of @sec-steric applied to ligand choice, and it returns in the TMA/DMAI comparison (@sec-tma-dmai).

### Simple, classic and complicated ligand families {#sec-ligand-tour}

It helps to sort ALD ligands into three tiers by how much design has gone into them:

- **Simple ligands** bond through a single atom and carry little or no organic framework: halides, hydrides and small alkyls. They are cheap, small and well understood, and they dominate industrial ALD.
- **Classic ligands** are the long-established families of organometallic and coordination chemistry: amides, alkoxides, cyclopentadienyls and β-diketonates. Their chemistry is mature, and their substituents can be varied to tune volatility and stability.
- **Complicated ligands** were designed, often for ALD specifically, to solve a problem the first two tiers could not: N,N-chelates such as amidinates, guanidinates and iminopyrrolidinates for low-valent metals; neutral donors such as carbenes and phosphines; and heteroleptic combinations in which each ligand has a job.

The tiers are a teaching device, not a rule: TMA is "simple" and still the best-behaved precursor known, while some "complicated" ligands were too costly to make on a large scale [@Barry2022].

| Tier | Family | Bonds through | Examples | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Simple | Halides | M–X (X = F, Cl, Br, I) | TiCl~4~, HfCl~4~, WF~6~ | Thermally robust; no carbon; cheap | Halide impurities at low temperature; corrosive HX by-products; often solids |
| Simple | Alkyls and hydrides | M–C, M–H | AlMe~3~, ZnEt~2~, GeH~2~Et~2~ | Very reactive; wide ALD windows | Often pyrophoric; transition-metal alkyls tend to decompose by β-H elimination |
| Classic | Amides, silylamides and imides | M–N | Ti(NMe~2~)~4~, Zn[N(SiMe~3~)~2~]~2~, W(N^t^Bu)~2~(NMe~2~)~2~ | No halides; reactive at low temperature | Limited thermal stability; silylamides leave Si; volatile mainly for high oxidation states |
| Classic | Alkoxides | M–O | Ti(O^i^Pr)~4~, Ta(OEt)~5~ | Thermally robust M–O bonds | Oligomerize unless bulky; can self-decompose; oxides only |
| Classic | Cyclopentadienyls | M–C (π) | RuCp~2~, ZrCp~2~Me~2~, InCp | Strong M–Cp bonding; substitution tunes volatility and melting point | Can still decompose at source temperatures; may stay on the surface |
| Classic | β-Diketonates | M–O (chelate) | M(acac)~n~, M(thd)~n~, M(hfac)~n~ | Robust; available for lanthanides, alkaline earths, noble metals | Low reactivity to water, usually need O~3~ or O~2~ |
| Complicated | N,N-chelates | M–N (chelate) | [Cu(^i^PrAMD)]~2~, La(^i^PrAMD)~3~ | Volatile, thermally stable compounds for many low-valent metals | Surface decomposition at higher temperatures; ligand-centred fragmentation |
| Complicated | Neutral donors (L) | M–CO, M–P, M–C (carbene) | W(CO)~6~, Au(PMe~3~)Me~3~, Cu(NHC)(N(SiMe~3~)~2~) | Stabilize low-valent metals; CO leaves cleanly | Carbonyls have low thermal stability; L-ligand loss complicates gas-phase chemistry |

: The main ALD ligand families, grouped into three tiers [@Barry2021; @Barry2022]. {#tbl-ligand-families tbl-colwidths="[11,14,12,19,20,24]"}

Two patterns are worth drawing out:

- **Stability versus reactivity.** The move from halides to alkylamides for high-k dielectrics removed chloride contamination and corrosive by-products and lowered deposition temperatures, but gave up thermal stability. The trade-off between halides and alkylamides is a clean case study of the tension described at the start of @sec-ligands.
- **Filling the low-oxidation-state gap.** Homoleptic dialkylamides of low-valent metals tend to oligomerize and decompose before they can be vaporized. Bidentate amidinates solved this, giving volatile, thermally stable compounds for many transition metals and lanthanum [@Lim2003]. Guanidinates extend the idea with an extra amino group on the central carbon [@Kurek2014].

Many modern precursors are **heteroleptic**: they combine different ligands so that one supplies stability and another supplies reactivity.

The gallery below shows representative precursors from each tier in three dimensions. Rotate them to see how much of each molecule is ligand: this is the bulk that sets steric saturation (@sec-steric) and that has to be removed cleanly in the next half-cycle.

Dimers are drawn with idealized D~2h~ cores. The script that builds them is `tools/build_ligand_gallery.py` in the source repository; add a molecule there to extend the gallery. Requires WebGL.

The sections that follow look at how each family reacts at the surface, using representative precursors from the AtomicLimits ALD Database as collected by @Barry2021.

#### Alkyls and hydrides

Alkyl precursors are the most studied class. They are straightforward to make and modify, and TMA/H~2~O is the prototypical ALD reaction [@Barry2021]. Representative alkyls span four decades: GaMe~3~ and AlMe~3~ with AsH~3~ for GaAs and AlAs (1985), SnMe~4~ for SnO~2~ (1994), ZnEt~2~ for Al-doped ZnO (1994), Pt(CpMe)Me~3~ with O~2~ for Pt (2003), and Au(PMe~3~)Me~3~ for Au (2016) [@Barry2021].

- **Chemisorption.** TMA reacts readily because Al is highly electropositive and has no accessible redox chemistry. The likely path is donation of the –OH lone pair into the empty p orbital on Al, followed by proton transfer to a methyl group, which leaves as CH~4~. TMA can bind to one –OH or to two neighbouring –OH groups (@sec-tma-model) [@Barry2021].
- **Oxidizing co-reactants.** With water, the surface methyls are simply protonated off. With ozone or an oxygen plasma, oxygen inserts into the Al–C bonds to give surface methoxy groups, which burn to bicarbonate and formate, release CO~2~, and leave –OH. Ethene is also observed [@Barry2021].
- **Metal surfaces.** On metals, the chemistry can differ. Au(PMe~3~)Me~3~ first loses its phosphine, and both fragments bind to the gold surface. RuCp(CO)~2~Et with O~2~ releases H~2~ as well as CO~2~ and H~2~O, and leaves a partial carbon layer that the next oxygen pulse removes [@Barry2021].
- **Hydrides.** Ge films from GeH~2~Et~2~ form by losing both hydrides on chemisorption, leaving an ethyl-terminated surface that is cleared by a temperature step. A mass-27 signal attributed to an ethyl radical (29 amu) is more plausibly ethene formed by β-H elimination [@Barry2021].

#### Cyclopentadienyls

Cp precursors were introduced in 1991, with much of the early development in Lauri Niinistö's group in Helsinki. Examples include MgCp~2~, ScCp~3~, YCp~3~, LaCp~3~ and Er(CpMe)~3~ with water for oxides, and RuCp~2~ and OsCp~2~ with O~2~ for metals [@Barry2021].

- **Combustion.** Ru from RuCp~2~ was first described as complete combustion of the ligands to CO~2~ and H~2~O; H~2~ was later found as a by-product too [@Barry2021].
- **Ligands left behind.** Metallocenes nucleate poorly on H-terminated silicon. In hydrogen, Cp can couple to dihydrofulvalene or be hydrogenated, which helps keep carbon out of Co films. NiCp~2~ with water, however, gives carbon-rich NiO, showing that some Cp can remain after chemisorption [@Barry2021].
- **Not every precursor loses a ligand on adsorption.** Mn(CpEt)~2~ appears to adsorb intact on a fluoride surface and only releases its Cp ligands during the HF-pyridine pulse [@Barry2021].
- **Half-sandwiches.** InCp is a coordination polymer in the solid but volatilizes as a monomer. It either reacts with –OH, eliminating CpH, or binds to surface oxygen while keeping its Cp ligand [@Barry2021].

#### Amides, silylamides and imides

The first amide precursor in ALD was Zn[N(SiMe~3~)~2~]~2~, used with H~2~Se for ZnSe in 1992 [@Barry2021]. Amides generally follow the same Brønsted acid–base chemistry as alkyls, releasing an amine on reaction with surface –OH or –NH~x~ groups.

- **Silylamides** (–N(SiMe~3~)~2~) are used across the periodic table, from Li and Zn to the lanthanides. With an oxygen source, the oxophilic silicon is scavenged into the film, giving a silicate [@Barry2021].
- **TiN from Ti(NR~2~)~4~ and NH~3~** involves a reduction from Ti(IV) to Ti(III). The often-quoted mechanism, which releases N~2~, has stoichiometric problems. A better explanation is β-H elimination to a surface imine, giving a formal Ti(II) that comproportionates with neighbouring Ti(IV) [@Barry2021]. With water, Ti stays at +4 and the film is TiO~2~.
- **Imido–amides**, M(NR)~x~(NR′~2~)~4−x~, are common for the refractory metals Nb, Mo, Ta and W. The strong M=N imido bond usually leads to nitride films [@Barry2021].

#### N,N-chelates

Amidinates (including guanidinates and iminopyrrolidinates) are the most important N,N-chelates. Their use traces back to one paper: in 2003, Gordon's group reported ALD of seven metals and oxides from amidinates [@Lim2003; @Barry2021]. Newer N,N-chelates include diazabutadienes, β-diketiminates (@sec-tunable-families) and triazenides [@Barry2021].

- **Heteroleptic precursors** let one ligand do the reacting. Al(^i^PrAMD)Et~2~ deposits Al~2~O~3~ with water down to 125 °C; solid-state NMR on the gallium analogue showed both ethyl groups are lost while the amidinate stays on the surface [@Barry2021].
- **Decomposition kinetics matter more than onset temperature.** On an ultraclean Ni surface in ultrahigh vacuum, the copper amidinate dimer starts decomposing at about −73 °C. Yet it gives self-limiting Cu ALD up to 280 °C. The difference is time: decomposition on Ni was followed over more than an hour, while an ALD pulse lasts seconds. Decomposition proceeds by β-H abstraction from the alkyl groups; replacing those H atoms with methyls raised thermal stability by more than 200 °C [@Barry2021].

#### Designing against decomposition: from guanidinates to iminopyrrolidinates {#sec-ip-design}

Amidinates and guanidinates have a low thermal threshold, and understanding why led directly to a better ligand [@Barry2013]. For Cu(I), Al(III) and Ga(III) compounds there are two main decomposition routes, and amidinates and guanidinates behave much the same way:

- **Carbodiimide deinsertion.** The reverse of the reaction used to make the ligand: a carbodiimide RN=C=NR is expelled, leaving the metal bonded to the former R or NR~2~ group. It tends to be a low-temperature, solution-phase route.
- **β-Hydrogen elimination.** A hydrogen on the carbon β to the metal (for example the methine H of an isopropyl group) is transferred, breaking up the ligand. It tends to be a higher-temperature, gas-phase route.

DFT calculations on the copper guanidinate dimer [Cu{(N^i^Pr)~2~CNMe~2~}]~2~ showed that both routes start from the **same intermediate** [@Barry2013]. One nitrogen shifts its bonding so that an isopropyl methine hydrogen points at copper, at a cost of about 94 kJ mol^−1^ (22.5 kcal mol^−1^). From there, deinsertion is slightly downhill (about −3 kJ mol^−1^), while β-H elimination is uphill overall (about 138 kJ mol^−1^) and needs the lattice energy of forming Cu metal to drive it. This explains the pattern: a solvent can stabilize the intermediate and open the easy deinsertion path, while in the gas phase or at a surface both routes compete [@Barry2013].

The redesign tackled each route in turn [@Barry2013]:

1. **Block deinsertion with a ring.** In an **iminopyrrolidinate** (ip), one bonding nitrogen and the bridging carbon sit in a five-membered ring, which makes carbodiimide deinsertion much less favourable. The ligands are made from commercial 2-pyrrolidone, in up to 87 % overall yield.
2. **Check what is left.** The Al(R-ip)Me~2~ family decomposed with half-lives of 1.8–24.8 days at 78 °C. The two fastest (R = ^i^Pr and ^s^Bu) still carry reactive β-hydrogens, so β-H elimination remained open.
3. **Remove the β-hydrogens.** In **tert-butyl-imino-2,2-dimethylpyrrolidinate** (Me~2~-^t^Bu-ip), the ring β-hydrogens are replaced by methyl groups and the imine carries a tert-butyl group, which has no β-hydrogens.

The copper compounds show the payoff:

| Ligand on [CuL]~2~ | Half-life at 165 °C (days) |
|:---|:---|
| Guanidinate, (^i^PrN)~2~CNMe~2~ | 1.4 |
| ^t^Bu-ip | 1.0 |
| ^i^Pr-ip | 7.5 |
| Me~2~-^t^Bu-ip | No measurable decomposition |

: Thermal stability of copper(I) compounds at 165 °C [@Barry2013]. {#tbl-cu-halflife}

On high-surface-area silica, [Cu(Me~2~-^t^Bu-ip)]~2~ chemisorbed as the dimer up to 275 °C, lost its tert-butyl group at 275 °C while remaining a stable monolayer, and only decomposed at 350 °C, leaving a diamine bound to copper [@Barry2013]. Compared with the guanidinate, which deposits copper metal by itself at 225 °C, the redesigned ligand raised the thermal limit by over 100 °C.

The general lesson is to identify the decomposition mechanism first, then design the ligand to close it off. The same mechanisms can also be exploited: copper guanidinates make effective single-source CVD precursors for copper metal precisely because they decompose cleanly at low temperature [@Barry2013].

The simulation below shows what these rate constants mean for a precursor held in a heated source. Assuming first-order decomposition, the fraction remaining after time t is exp(−kt).

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.10: How long does a precursor survive in a hot source?]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ipData = [
  {set: "Cu(I) at 165 °C", name: "[Cu(guanidinate)]₂", k: 0.49},
  {set: "Cu(I) at 165 °C", name: "[Cu(ᵗBu-ip)]₂", k: 0.71},
  {set: "Cu(I) at 165 °C", name: "[Cu(ⁱPr-ip)]₂", k: 0.092},
  {set: "Cu(I) at 165 °C", name: "[Cu(Me₂-ᵗBu-ip)]₂", k: 0},
  {set: "Al(R-ip)Me₂ at 78 °C", name: "R = ⁱPr", k: 0.382},
  {set: "Al(R-ip)Me₂ at 78 °C", name: "R = ⁿPr", k: 0.124},
  {set: "Al(R-ip)Me₂ at 78 °C", name: "R = ⁿBu", k: 0.028},

]
viewof ipSet = Inputs.radio(["Cu(I) at 165 °C", "Al(R-ip)Me₂ at 78 °C"], {value: "Cu(I) at 165 °C", label: "Compound series"})
```

```{ojs}
}))

Plot.plot({
```

```{ojs}
})), {format: {
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** First-order decomposition with the rate constants measured at a single temperature [@Barry2013]; "no measurable decomposition" is plotted as k = 0. The dotted line marks 2 % loss: one patent specification for Group 11 precursors asks for less than about 2 % decomposition after a week at about 10 °C above the source temperature. Real sources also see temperature gradients, repeated heating cycles and impurities, all of which can speed up decomposition.
:::
:::

#### Alkoxides and β-diketonates

Alkoxides have been used for about 30 years, mainly for oxides, because the strong M–O bonds tend to leave oxygen in the film. Much of their early development was done by Leskelä and Ritala at the University of Helsinki [@Barry2021]. They are particularly useful for mixed oxides such as perovskites. In one striking case, Te metal is deposited from Te(SiMe~3~)~2~ and Te(OEt)~4~: the oxophilic silicon pulls the ethoxide off as Me~3~SiOEt, leaving Te^0^ in both half-cycles [@Barry2021].

β-Diketonates (acac, thd, hfac and others) often **chemisorb as the ligand** rather than leaving as the free diketone, possibly because their conjugate acids are much more acidic than those of other ligands [@Barry2021]. The surface-bound ligand can then be combusted, which allows metal films of Pt, Cu, Ir and Rh. Fluorinated hfac rarely leaves fluorine in the film, but it has also been used deliberately as a fluorine source: CaF~2~ was grown from Ca(thd)~2~ and O~3~ alternated with H(hfac) [@Barry2021].

#### Neutral donor ligands

L ligands are less common in ALD, but they appear in several important precursors [@Barry2021]:

- **Carbonyls** are rare and mostly found in heteroleptic compounds. Their main weakness is low thermal stability: CoCp(CO)~2~ is far more volatile than CoCp~2~, but it loses CO in the gas phase, which suits CVD rather than ALD. W(CO)~6~ with NH~3~ gives WN~x~ by CO loss with < 1 % carbon. On hydroxylated oxides, Mo(CO)~6~ shows complex redox chemistry that depends on the –OH density.
- **Phosphines** stabilize low-valent and noble-metal precursors, as in Au(PMe~3~)Me~3~ above.
- **N-heterocyclic carbenes** (NHCs) are strong σ-donors, used for example in Cu(^i^Pr~2~-NHC)(N(SiMe~3~)~2~) for Cu films.

#### Which ligand leaves first?

For a heteroleptic precursor, a first guess is that the ligand with the **least acidic conjugate acid** is the most basic, and so is protonated and lost first at a surface –OH. Approximate pK~a~ values of some conjugate acids are:

| Ligand | Conjugate acid | Approximate pK~a~ |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Methyl | CH~4~ | ~50 |
| Dialkylamide | HNR~2~ | ~35–40 |
| Alkoxide | ROH | ~16–18 |
| Cyclopentadienyl | C~5~H~6~ | ~16 |
| β-Diketonate | β-diketone | ~9 |
| Chloride | HCl | ~ −7 |

: Approximate pK~a~ values of ligand conjugate acids. {#tbl-pka}

On this basis, ZrCp~2~Me~2~ should lose its methyl groups and keep its Cp ligands. Mass spectrometry shows that it loses both, with methyl loss dominant but CpH also released [@Barry2021]. The reason is that ALD surface reactions are **not at equilibrium**: the leaving ligand is swept away by the gas flow, so less favourable pathways can compete. Tying the two Cp rings together (an *ansa*-zirconocene) brings in the chelate effect, and then only the methyls are lost [@Barry2021]. pK~a~ is a useful first guess, not a prediction.

## Precursors {#sec-precursors}

[Applies to: ALD · MLD · ALE · ASD]{.applies}

Every gas-phase reactant in an atomic layer process is a precursor: the metal precursor and the water in ALD, the organic linker in MLD, the modification and removal reagents in ALE, and the inhibitor in ASD. The requirements below were worked out for ALD metal precursors, but the same questions (is it volatile, is it stable, does it react once and stop?) apply to all of them.

### What is a precursor?

Strictly, every gas-phase reactant in an ALD process is a precursor, and every one should be shown to be self-limiting [@Barry2022]. By tradition, though, the compound that carries the metal (the **payload** atom, such as Al in Al~2~O~3~) is called "the precursor", and the other is called the "co-reactant" or named for its role: oxidant, reducing agent, nitrogen source. The co-reactant often decides the film and so defines the chemistry of the cycle [@Barry2022].

Labels like "oxidant" can mislead. Ozone is a good example, because it reacts in at least three different ways [@Barry2022]:

- **With Mo(CO)~6~**, molybdenum goes from 0 to +6. Here ozone really is an oxidant, and the CO ligands may be oxidized to CO~2~ as well.
- **With AlCl~3~**, aluminum is +3 before and after. Ozone supplies oxygen but oxidizes nothing at the metal; the by-product is likely a reactive chlorine oxide.
- **With a Au(III) precursor**, ozone combusts the ligands and the gold ends up as Au(0), a formal *reduction*. Ozone did not reduce the gold: gold, being noble, prefers the zero oxidation state and takes electrons during the combustion.

Surface reactions can go down many pathways at once. This is one reason simple, small precursors with well-defined reactivity are preferred: one pathway is more likely to dominate [@Barry2022].

### How precursors react

#### Brønsted acid–base chemisorption

Most metal precursors react rapidly with air and moisture. This is deliberate: the same reactivity that forms an extended solid in ALD also makes the compound air-sensitive [@Barry2022]. The most common surface reaction is a proton transfer from a surface site to a ligand:

$$
\text{MX}_n + \|\!-\!\text{EH} \rightarrow \|\!-\!\text{E–MX}_{n-1} + \text{HX}
$$ {#eq-acidbase}

Here ‖–EH is a nucleation site such as ‖–OH on an oxide or ‖–NH~2~ on a nitride, and the ligand X acts as a Brønsted base, leaving as its conjugate acid HX [@Barry2022]. This reaction is the usual starting point when designing a precursor, which is why halide and alkyl precursors dominate.

**Halides.** Metal halides are thermally stable, simple to make from the metal or its oxide, and volatile enough to be purified by distillation or sublimation, even on a large scale [@Barry2022]. Their by-product, HX, is a strong acid that can corrode equipment and etch films.

**Alkyls.** With an alkyl, the by-product is a very stable alkane. Carbon contamination is then more likely to come from alkyl groups left *on* the surface than from the one that leaves [@Barry2022]. The by-product can be remarkably benign. When Beneq installed a TMA/H~2~O process at a Helsinki jewellery shop in the early 2000s to stop silver from tarnishing, it showed the authorities that a typical run released less methane than a cow does in a day [@Barry2022]. The cost is that alkyls are much more reactive towards water and less thermally stable than halides: they allow lower process temperatures, but give messy, CVD-like growth at higher ones [@Barry2022].

#### Chemisorption versus physisorption

AlCl~3~ shows the difference. In the gas phase it is in equilibrium between the Al~2~Cl~6~ dimer and the monomer; higher temperatures favour the monomer, which reacts faster, so the dimer can slow saturation slightly [@Barry2022]. At the surface:

- **Chemisorption** by @eq-acidbase is strong and effectively permanent. Having lost an X ligand, the surface species cannot simply desorb, because it would have to leave as a cation.
- **Physisorption** happens when the Lewis-acidic monomer accepts electron density from a surface oxygen through a weak dative bond. A physisorbed AlCl~3~ can easily return to the gas phase [@Barry2022].

#### Combustion

Less commonly, the precursor reacts by oxidation, for example with O~2~ as the co-reactant. RuO~2~ can be grown from Ru(CpEt)~2~ and O~2~. Written as a complete combustion [@Barry2022]:

$$
2\,\text{Ru(CpEt)}_2 + 39\,\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\,\text{RuO}_2 + 28\,\text{CO}_2 + 18\,\text{H}_2\text{O}
$$ {#eq-ru-combustion}

Nearly 20 O~2~ molecules are needed for each Ru atom, so combustion is often incomplete, giving CO and partly oxidized fragments. The water produced can also hydroxylate the surface and help the next cycle nucleate [@Barry2022]. In situ mass spectrometry of Ru and Pt ALD shows that the oxygen pulse leaves a layer of adsorbed oxygen, which then burns the ligands of the incoming precursor to CO~2~ and H~2~O [@Aaltonen2003]. Ozone combusts ligands too: with TMA, oxygen inserts into the Al–CH~3~ bonds to give surface methoxy and formate species before CO~2~ is released [@Goldstein2008].

### Making precursors

Two reactions do most of the work in laboratory-scale precursor synthesis [@Barry2022].

**Salt metathesis** exchanges ligands between a metal halide and a ligand salt, often a lithium reagent:

$$
\text{ZnCl}_2 + 2\,\text{LiEt} \rightarrow \text{ZnEt}_2 + 2\,\text{LiCl}
$$ {#eq-metathesis}

The reaction is run in a solvent in which LiCl is insoluble. The salt precipitates and leaves the solution, so the equilibrium keeps shifting towards products until the reaction is complete.

**Elimination of a volatile product** works the same way. Diethylzinc reacts with acetic acid to give zinc acetate (a precursor for ZnS) and ethane gas, which bubbles out of the solution:

$$
\text{ZnEt}_2 + 2\,\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \rightarrow \text{Zn(O}_2\text{CCH}_3)_2 + 2\,\text{C}_2\text{H}_6
$$ {#eq-elimination}

The leaving group does not have to be an alkane; any ligand whose protonated form is volatile will do. Both reactions are applications of Le Chatelier's principle: removing a product drives the equilibrium to completion [@Barry2022]. A third route, insertion of a carbodiimide into a metal–alkyl or metal–amide bond, makes the amidinates and guanidinates discussed in @sec-ip-design.

### Designing precursors {#sec-designing-precursors}

#### What a precursor needs

For a precursor to give ALD, it must be [@Barry2022]:

1. Volatile
2. Thermally stable
3. Reactive with the substrate and the growing film
4. Self-limiting
5. Reactive towards the second precursor

Each property can be optimized on its own; the art of precursor design is to improve one without sacrificing another. For industrial use, a precursor must also be easy to make, scalable, safe to handle and inexpensive [@Barry2022]. These requirements differ from those for CVD, where the precursor is meant to keep decomposing: an ALD precursor must survive the deposition temperature and react only with surface groups and the co-reactant [@Leskela1999; @Leskela2003]. In practice these requirements map onto specific tests:

| Requirement | Why it matters | How it is tested |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Volatility | Enough vapour to saturate the surface in a short pulse | Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), vapour pressure |
| Thermal stability (source and reactor) | Decomposition breaks self-limitation and adds impurities | TGA residue, long-term ageing at source temperature, NMR after heating |
| Self-limiting reactivity | The precursor must chemisorb, then stop | Saturation curves (@sec-what-makes-ald) |
| Complete reaction with the co-reactant | Low impurity levels | Film composition (XPS, ERDA) |
| Benign by-products | Volatile, non-etching, not re-adsorbed | Mass spectrometry of the exhaust |
| Matching oxidation state | Avoids an extra redox step | Compare metal oxidation state in precursor and film |
| Physical state | Liquids deliver vapour more steadily than solids | Melting point |

: Precursor requirements and how they are tested. {#tbl-requirements}
