**Oxidation state.** Ideally, the metal's oxidation state is the same in the precursor and the film. Ta(NMe~2~)~5~ contains Ta(V) and gives insulating Ta~3~N~5~ by default; conductive TaN needs Ta(III), so a reduction step is required. Metal films are the extreme case, needing M^n+^ → M^0^. For electropositive first-row transition metals this requires strong reducing co-reactants and remains one of the hardest problems in ALD precursor chemistry [@Knisley2013; @Emslie2013].

**How stable is stable enough?** One patent for Group 11 precursors specifies less than about 2 % decomposition by weight (preferably less than 1 %) after one week at about 10 °C above the ALD source temperature [@Barry2016patent]. Simulation 2.10 shows what this means in terms of rate constants. Industrial suppliers screen new precursors in the same spirit, using TGA and NMR after extended heating to decide whether a compound is safe to use in production equipment [@Rushworth2007].

#### Volatility

A precursor needs to vaporize at a low temperature, and fast enough to keep pulses short [@Barry2022].

##### The molecular-weight myth

A common idea is that lighter molecules are more volatile. It comes from the Knudsen effusion equation, which relates the mass loss Δm through an orifice of area A~o~ in time Δt to the vapour pressure p~v~:

$$
p_\text{v} = \frac{\Delta m}{A_\text{o}\,\Delta t}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi RT}{M}}
$$ {#eq-knudsen}

The M^−1/2^ dependence describes how fast molecules escape once they are in the gas, assuming ideal, non-interacting molecules. That assumption is reasonable in a dilute gas but fails in the condensed phase, where intermolecular interactions decide whether a molecule can leave at all [@Barry2022]. Lighter molecules often have fewer ways to interact, so molecular weight correlates with volatility, but it is not the cause.

##### Thermodynamics of evaporation

Evaporation and sublimation are always **endothermic** (ΔH~vap~ > 0), and always increase entropy (ΔS~vap~ > 0). From ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, vaporization becomes favourable once TΔS outweighs ΔH. A volatile precursor therefore needs a **small enthalpy of vaporization** and a **large entropy of vaporization** [@Barry2022]. The equilibrium vapour pressure follows the Clausius–Clapeyron form:

$$
\ln\frac{p}{p^\circ} = -\frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{RT} + \frac{\Delta S_\text{vap}}{R}
$$ {#eq-cc}

with p° = 1 bar. Simulation 2.12 in @sec-volatility-control uses this equation to find the source temperature for a given vapour pressure.

##### Controlling intermolecular interactions

Lowering ΔH~vap~ means weakening the interactions between molecules: electrostatic, hydrogen bonding, dipole–dipole, ion–dipole and van der Waals [@Barry2022].

- **Bond polarity.** Polar bonds strengthen intermolecular interactions. AlCl~3~ (Δχ(Al–Cl) = 1.55) is less volatile than TMA (Δχ(Al–C) = 0.94) [@Barry2022].
- **Hydrocarbon shells.** Non-polar alkyl groups on the ligand periphery shield the polar core of the molecule.
- **Fluorination.** Fluorine holds its electrons tightly and is hard to polarize, so replacing CH~3~ with CF~3~ weakens intermolecular interactions. In a series of β-diketonate dimethylgold(III) compounds sharing the same framework, volatility at 25 °C increases with each CF~3~ group, while the decomposition temperature stays the same [@Barry2022]. The trade-off is a greater risk of fluorine in the film.

#### Thermal stability

Thermal stability comes down to the strength of the bonds between the payload atom and its ligands [@Barry2022]:

- **Electropositive metals** (Al, Zn, Ti) form strong bonds to oxygen, so O-donor ligands give stable precursors. The price is oxygen in the film, and metal films of these elements are very hard to make.
- **Electronegative, noble metals** (Au, Pt, Pd) form weak bonds to oxygen, so O-donor precursors tend to be unstable. Their oxides are also hard to make: with water, O~2~ or O~3~ as the co-reactant, these metals usually give metallic films.

Design for stability follows two paths: use chelating ligands, and design out low-temperature decomposition pathways [@Barry2022].

##### Chelation

TTIP, Ti(O^i^Pr)~4~, switches from ALD to CVD growth at 240 °C. In Ti(thd)~2~(O^i^Pr)~2~, all bonds to Ti(IV) are still to oxygen, but two of the ligands are chelating β-diketonates. Surface decomposition then starts at 380 °C, 140 °C higher [@Barry2022]. The thermodynamics of chelation are covered in @sec-chelate.

##### Designing out decomposition pathways

The common decomposition pathways are:

- **β-Hydrogen elimination**, in which a hydrogen two bonds away from the metal is transferred to the metal, giving a metal hydride and an alkene (or an imine, for alkylamides). Ligands with β-hydrogens and coordinatively unsaturated metals are most at risk.
- **Ligand fragmentation**, such as carbodiimide deinsertion from amidinates and guanidinates, or C–N, C–O and N–N bond cleavage.
- **Redox reactions**, such as disproportionation of Cu(I) or Au(I).
- **Surface-catalysed decomposition**: metals and reducible oxides lower decomposition barriers compared with the gas phase.

Gold shows how far redesign can go. An early Au(I) guanidinate gave CVD at 150 °C with a growth rate of 39 nm min^−1^, useless for ALD. It decomposed by both carbodiimide deinsertion and β-H elimination. Switching to the iminopyrrolidinate tert-butyl-imino-2,2-dimethylpyrrolidinate, which blocks deinsertion and has no β-hydrogens, gave a gold(I) compound that does not decompose below 275 °C, compared with 150 °C for the guanidinate; in CVD experiments, gas-phase decomposition was observed at about 300 °C [@Coyle2013; @Barry2022]. The new ligand was too costly to make industrially, which illustrates another design rule: **keep it simple** [@Barry2022]. The same strategy for copper is described in @sec-ip-design.

#### Melting point

A low melting point is not essential, but a liquid source improves reproducibility [@Barry2022]. A liquid's surface area stays constant and surface impurities are mobile. A solid's surface area shrinks as its particles evaporate, and impurities collect on it, so the vapour delivered can fall over the life of the source. On the other hand, solids are safer to ship and easier to load. The ideal precursor melts **above** shipping and handling temperatures but **below** the source temperature [@Barry2022].

Melting points can be tuned. Long, unbranched alkyl chains frustrate crystallization because they can adopt many conformations. Tungsten hexacarbonyl shows why this matters: as a solid it is not a reproducible vapour source, because its surface area changes as it evaporates, and its vapour is toxic [@Gordon2000]. W(CO)~6~ melts at 170 °C; replacing one CO with an isonitrile, CNR, gives W(CO)~5~(CNR), which melts below 100 °C. As R grows from C~3~ to C~5~, the melting point falls roughly linearly to below 0 °C, suggesting a butyl chain would give a solid at room temperature that melts in the source. There is no further gain at C~6~, and with C~8~ the melting point rises again to about 20 °C [@Barry2022]. With suitable alkyl groups these compounds are low-viscosity liquids at room temperature, suitable for liquid delivery [@Gordon2000].

#### Reactivity and heteroleptic design

A precursor must react with the surface and the co-reactant (intermolecular reactivity) without reacting with itself (intramolecular reactivity) [@Barry2022]. Heteroleptic precursors split these jobs: one ligand anchors the precursor to the surface, and another stays on the metal and protects it.

The pK~a~ of each ligand's conjugate acid is a first guide to which ligand will act as the anchor (@sec-ligand-tour): the most basic ligand, whose conjugate acid has the highest pK~a~, is the most likely to take a proton from the surface. In MeAlCl~2~, for example, the methyl group (pK~a~ of CH~4~ ≈ 50) reacts with a surface –OH, and the chlorides (pK~a~ of HCl ≈ −7) stay on the chemisorbed aluminum [@Barry2022]. Choosing which ligand reacts lets a chemist choose what is left on the surface for the next half-cycle.

### Case study: TMA versus DMAI {#sec-tma-dmai}

<!-- TODO(SB): add measured vapour pressure, GPC, temperature range and impurity data for TMA vs DMAI from L3, and the primary references. The predictions below are deliberately qualitative until then. -->

Dimethylaluminum isopropoxide, [Me~2~Al(μ-O^i^Pr)]~2~ (DMAI), has been explored as an alternative to TMA for Al~2~O~3~. It differs from TMA by one ligand: an isopropoxide in place of a methyl. That single change touches every requirement in @tbl-requirements, which makes the pair a good exercise in using the principles of this chapter. Look at both molecules in Simulation 2.9 before reading on.

| | TMA, Al~2~Me~6~ ⇌ 2 AlMe~3~ | DMAI, [Me~2~Al(O^i^Pr)]~2~ |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Bridging ligand in the dimer | Methyl, 3c–2e bond (weak) | Alkoxide oxygen, lone-pair donation (strong) |
| Coordination at Al | 3 in the monomer, so strongly Lewis acidic | 4 in the dimer |
| Most basic ligand (anchor) | CH~3~^−^ (CH~4~, pK~a~ ≈ 50) | CH~3~^−^; the O^i^Pr (pK~a~ of ^i^PrOH ≈ 17) is a much weaker base |
| Al content (monomer formula) | 37 % by mass | 23 % by mass |
| β-Hydrogens | None | Yes, on the isopropoxide |

: TMA and DMAI compared from their structures. {#tbl-tma-dmai}

From these differences, the principles in this chapter predict:

- **Volatility.** The alkoxide bridge is a lone-pair donation, like the chloride bridge in Al~2~Cl~6~, and is stronger than TMA's methyl bridge. DMAI should be a more robust dimer, with a larger enthalpy of vaporization, so it needs a heated source where TMA does not.
- **Handling.** Monomeric TMA has an exposed, three-coordinate Al, which is why it is pyrophoric. In DMAI, the oxygen bridges keep Al four-coordinate, so it should react less violently with air and moisture. This is the main practical argument for it.
- **Chemisorption.** By the pK~a~ argument (@tbl-pka), the methyl groups react with surface –OH and the isopropoxide stays on the chemisorbed aluminum until the water pulse removes it as isopropanol.
- **Growth per cycle.** A surface fragment that keeps an isopropoxide is larger than one that keeps a methyl, so steric saturation (@sec-steric) should set in at fewer Al per nm^2^. Expect a lower GPC than TMA at the same temperature.
- **Upper temperature limit.** The isopropoxide carries β-hydrogens, which opens β-H elimination (to propene and an Al–H or Al–OH) at high temperature: a route to a CVD component that TMA does not have.
- **Payload.** With less Al per gram, more precursor is consumed per unit of film, which matters for cost and for the figure of merit in @sec-fom.

Each prediction is testable with the tools in @sec-thermolysis and a saturation curve. Note what the comparison does *not* say: neither molecule is simply "better". TMA should win on volatility, GPC and simplicity; DMAI's case rests on safety and handling. As with TMA and AlCl~3~ (@tbl-tma-alcl3), the choice depends on what the application can tolerate.

### Second precursors {#sec-second-precursors}

The co-reactant sets the film's anion (or reduces the metal), removes the remaining ligands and regenerates reactive surface sites.

| Film | Typical co-reactants |
|:---|:---|
| Metal oxide | H~2~O, O~3~, O~2~ (thermal or plasma) |
| Metal nitride | NH~3~, hydrazines and amines, N~2~/H~2~ plasma |
| Metal sulfide, selenide, telluride | H~2~S, H~2~Se, H~2~Te (toxic), or E(SiMe~3~)~2~ with metal chlorides |
| Metal fluoride | HF–pyridine, TiF~4~, TaF~5~ |
| Elemental metal | Reducing agents; O~2~ or O~3~ for noble metals only |

: Co-reactants by film type. {#tbl-coreactants}

The three common oxygen sources behave very differently:

| | H~2~O | O~3~ | O~2~ plasma |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Mechanism | Protonolysis; regenerates –OH | Combusts ligands; can oxidize the substrate | Combustion by O radicals and ions |
| Works with | Alkyls, amides, halides | Also β-diketonates and Cp, which react poorly with water | Most precursors |
| Temperature | Moderate | Lower possible | Lowest |
| Typical issues | Slow purges at low temperature; hygroscopic films | Carbonate and carbon impurities; substrate oxidation | Plasma damage; lower conformality |

: Oxygen co-reactants compared [@Goldstein2008; @Profijt2011]. {#tbl-oxygen-sources}

A weaker co-reactant can even **create selectivity**. O~2~ dissociates readily only on noble metals, so a metal oxide can be grown on Pt while not growing on SiO~2~ or Al~2~O~3~. Stronger oxidants such as O~3~ or an oxygen plasma react on any surface and remove that selectivity [@Singh2018].

The common second precursors each bring their own chemistry:

- **Water** reacts by protonolysis: it protonates the remaining ligands off as their conjugate acids and leaves the surface hydroxylated for the next cycle. Its weakness is that it sticks to everything, including the reactor walls, so it needs long purges, especially at low temperature. In a typical showerhead reactor depositing Al~2~O~3~, a water purge is of the order of 10 s, while ozone can be cleared in about 1 s [@Barry2022]. Water that is not purged meets the next metal precursor pulse and adds a CVD component.
- **Ozone** decomposes to O~2~ and atomic oxygen, and either can react at the surface. Rather than simply protonating the ligands, it inserts oxygen into metal–carbon and C–H bonds and then burns the ligands to CO, CO~2~ and water through methoxy, formate and bicarbonate intermediates (@sec-migratory-insertion) [@Barry2022; @Goldstein2008]. It works with ligands that react poorly with water, such as β-diketonates and Cp, but can leave carbonate impurities and oxidize the substrate.
- **Plasmas** supply radicals, ions and photons. An O~2~ plasma reacts largely through O radicals, so the chemistry is close to that of ozone [@Barry2022]. H~2~ plasmas supply atomic hydrogen for metals; N~2~/H~2~ and NH~3~ plasmas are used for nitrides. Plasmas allow much lower temperatures, but radicals recombine on the walls of deep features, which limits conformality, and ions can damage the film or substrate [@Profijt2011].
- **Ammonia** is the usual nitrogen source. It leaves ‖–NH~x~ groups that act as nucleation sites for the next metal pulse (@sec-surfaces). For many nitrides the metal must also be reduced, Ti(IV) to Ti(III) in TiN for example, and this needs a surface redox step such as reductive elimination (@sec-reductive-elimination).
- **Reducing agents** are needed when the film is a metal and the metal is not noble. Molecular H~2~ often reacts only on a catalytically active metal surface, H~2~ plasma supplies atomic hydrogen, and metal reductants such as zinc vapour or diethylzinc reduce by ligand exchange [@Barry2022]. For electropositive first-row metals this is still one of the hardest problems in ALD precursor chemistry [@Knisley2013; @Emslie2013]. Noble metals are the exception: they grow with O~2~, by combustion of the ligands, because their oxides are unstable.

## Thermolysis and thermal characterization {#sec-thermolysis}

[Applies to: ALD · MLD · ALE · ASD]{.applies}

What a precursor does at the surface depends on the process: the target film, the second precursor, the temperature. Two properties do not. A precursor must be volatile at a useful temperature, and it must not react with itself in that range. There is no process at all without both, which makes them the first things to measure [@Barry2022].

Neither property has an on/off temperature. Evaporation and decomposition are both reactions with their own kinetics, and both speed up as the temperature rises. The useful question is not "at what temperature does it start?" but "at what temperature does it become fast enough to matter over the timescale of a pulse, or of a week in a heated source?" [@Barry2022].

### Thermal onset temperatures

Two working definitions make the question answerable [@Barry2022]:

- **T~V~, the volatilization temperature**: the lowest temperature at which the precursor gives enough vapour for a process. A common choice is the temperature at which the vapour pressure reaches 1 Torr (133 Pa). This suits flow reactors, where carrier gases are typically at 1–5 Torr and the precursor is then not overly diluted.
- **T~D~, the decomposition temperature**: the highest temperature at which thermal decomposition can be ignored. The decomposition that matters here happens before or during volatilization, so T~D~ is effectively the highest safe source ("bubbler") temperature. It says nothing directly about decomposition at the substrate, which can be catalysed by the surface (@sec-au-120).

### Thermogravimetric analysis {#sec-tga}

Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) follows the mass of a sample on a microbalance while a furnace runs a temperature programme. The standard screening experiment for a new precursor loads 10–50 mg and ramps the temperature at a constant rate, usually 10 °C min^−1^ [@Barry2022]. A precursor that volatilizes cleanly shows three things:

1. **One thermal event**: a single, smooth mass-loss step with no inflections.
2. **An exponential onset** in the derivative of the mass-loss curve (DTG), which then drops sharply to zero when the sample is gone.
3. **Zero residual mass.**

None of these is proof, but a trace with all three is encouraging [@Barry2022]. Three refinements turn the screening run into a better test:

- **Change the ramp rate.** At a slower ramp, the sample spends longer at each temperature. A compound with a slow decomposition leaves more residue; one that does not decompose simply loses its mass at a lower apparent onset temperature and over a steeper step. This is one reason not to trust the "onset" of a TGA trace as a material property: it depends on ramp rate and sample mass [@Barry2022]. (Whether a slower ramp raises the residue also depends on how steeply decomposition speeds up with temperature compared with evaporation: if decomposition has the higher activation energy, a slower ramp lets the sample evaporate before it gets hot, and the residue falls.)
- **Change the sample mass (the thermal stress test).** The evaporation rate is set by the pan area, not by the sample mass, so a larger sample is still in the pan at higher temperatures. Repeating the ramp at several masses exposes slow decomposition: in one example, the residue rose from 2 % for about 10 mg to 14 % for about 60 mg [@Barry2022]. A precursor like that would be a risk in a source held at moderate temperature for days or weeks.
- **Run it isothermally.** An isothermal run gives the delivery rate at one temperature. Because the purge gas sweeps vapour away, evaporation never reaches equilibrium (Le Chatelier's principle again), so a TGA can overestimate the vapour pressure that would build up in a closed source. For ranking similar precursors, and as a model of a pulse that also removes vapour, it is still very useful [@Barry2022].

A careful vapour-pressure measurement uses a **stepped isotherm**: the temperature is raised in increments (for example 5 °C) and held at each step until the mass loss is linear, giving a rate Δm/Δt at each temperature. The Langmuir vapour-pressure equation, from kinetic gas theory, then gives

$$
p_\text{vap} = \frac{1}{\alpha}\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi RT}{M}} = k\,\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}\sqrt{\frac{T}{M}}
$$ {#eq-langmuir-vp}

where α corrects for non-ideal behaviour (α = 1 in vacuum). In practice, the whole prefactor k is calibrated against a standard of known vapour pressure [@Barry2022]. A plot of ln p~vap~ against 1/T then follows the Clausius–Clapeyron equation (@eq-cc): its slope gives ΔH~vap~, and reading off 1 Torr gives T~V~. If several related precursors give parallel lines, they share their volatilization thermodynamics; one that does not is worth a closer look [@Barry2022].

### Diagnosing decomposition from mass loss {#sec-tga-decomposition}

A TGA trace records a race between two ways of losing mass. **Evaporation** removes intact molecules at a rate set by the vapour pressure and the area of the pan; it does not depend on how much sample is left, so it is zero order in sample mass. **Decomposition** is a reaction of whatever is still in the pan; it is (usually) first order in that mass, and its products split between gases that leave and solids that stay. Diagnosing decomposition means working out which process won, at what temperature, and what was left behind. Five pieces of evidence do most of the work.

#### 1. Compare the residue with the payload

The first number to calculate for any new precursor is the mass percentage of the payload atom, %m~M~ (@eq-fom). If a precursor decomposes completely in the pan, the ligands leave as volatile fragments and the payload stays, so the residual mass lands near %m~M~, or near the mass percentage of the oxide, nitride or carbide if heteroatoms are retained. Calculate all the plausible phases before you look at the trace. For a tin compound of molar mass 400 g mol^−1^, tin is 29.7 % of the mass and SnO~2~ would be 37.7 %. A residue near one of these numbers, and *independent of sample mass*, says that most of the sample decomposed before it could evaporate. A residue that is larger than any plausible payload phase means ligand fragments or carbon were left behind as well.

The reverse does not hold. A residue near zero shows that nothing involatile was left; it does not show that the molecule that left was the one you loaded (point 2).

#### 2. Count the steps and measure them

A clean precursor gives one step. Two or more steps, separated by a plateau or an inflection, mean that the sample changed into something else part-way through the run [@Barry2022]. The size of the first step is a stoichiometry measurement: compare it with the molar masses of the ligands, or the fragments, that the molecule could lose.

Aluminium tris(amidinate)s are a worked case. For [MeC(N^i^Pr)~2~]~3~Al (M = 450.7 g mol^−1^), loss of one *N*,*N*′-diisopropylcarbodiimide (^i^PrN=C=N^i^Pr, 126.2 g mol^−1^) by deinsertion (@sec-ip-design) would remove 28.0 % of the mass. When these compounds were heated in a TGA and the condensed off-gas was examined by NMR, carbodiimide deinsertion turned out to be the main decomposition route of the homoleptic tris(amidinate)s, with onsets of only 88–120 °C. A heteroleptic dimethyl compound with an ethyl-substituted amidinate, EtC(N^i^Pr)~2~AlMe~2~, volatilized cleanly below 210 °C with no carbodiimide detected [@Brazeau2006]. The calculation tells you what to look for; collecting what leaves the pan tells you whether you were right.

#### 3. Read the shape of the derivative

Evaporation and decomposition leave different shapes in the DTG (the derivative, −dm/dT). Because evaporation is limited by the pan area and the vapour pressure rises exponentially, the DTG of a volatilizing sample rises exponentially and then drops to zero the moment the pan is empty: a cliff. Decomposition slows down as the reactant is used up, so its DTG is a rounded, more nearly symmetric peak [@Barry2013]. The distinction is easiest to see in a single, well-separated event, and it blurs when both processes run at once.

#### 4. Change the sample mass

The thermal stress test (@sec-tga) is the most reliable single check for *slow* decomposition, because it does not depend on how the two activation energies compare. A larger sample stays in the pan longer and reaches higher temperatures before it has all evaporated, so a precursor that decomposes slowly leaves more residue as the sample mass increases. A precursor that does not decompose leaves the same, near-zero residue at every mass [@Barry2013; @Barry2022]. Changing the ramp rate is less reliable: whether a slower ramp raises or lowers the residue depends on whether decomposition or evaporation speeds up faster with temperature.

The step also moves to higher temperature as the sample gets larger, with or without decomposition. On its own, that shift is the pan-area effect, not a sign of trouble.

#### 5. Hold the temperature

At constant temperature, evaporation from a fixed area gives a constant rate: mass falls in a straight line until the pan is empty. Decomposition bends the line, because its rate falls as the reactant is consumed, and the run ends on a plateau at the residual mass rather than at zero. A conversion like carbodiimide loss levels off at the mass of the product. Holds at several temperatures give decomposition rate constants, and from those an activation energy and a half-life at the source temperature [@Barry2022].

Half-lives turn a TGA result into a process decision. A copper(I) guanidinate dimer has a half-life of 1.41 days at 165 °C (k = 0.49 day^−1^); after a week at that temperature, only 3 % of the loaded precursor would be intact. Its redesigned iminopyrrolidinate analogue, [Cu(Me~2~-^t^Bu-ip)]~2~, showed no measurable decomposition at the same temperature [@Barry2013]. Simulation 2.10 plots these numbers.

#### What a TGA cannot see

TGA weighs what stays in the pan, so it is blind to some decomposition that matters:

- **Decomposition after evaporation**, in the gas phase or on the hot walls of a delivery line.
- **Surface-catalysed decomposition** on the substrate, which can happen well below any temperature at which the pure precursor decomposes (@sec-au-120).
- **Slow decomposition over days or weeks** in a heated source. A ramp lasts about half an hour; a bubbler runs for weeks (@sec-decomposition-testing, [@Kim2022]).

When the mass-loss evidence is ambiguous, identify what leaves the pan. TGA coupled to a mass spectrometer or an FTIR identifies evolved gases as they form, and for air-sensitive precursors the balance can be housed in a glovebox so the sample never sees air. Condensing the off-gas and running its NMR spectrum is a simple alternative [@Brazeau2006].

| What you see | Most likely reading | Next experiment |
|---|---|---|
| One step, DTG cliff, ≈0 % residue at every mass | Clean volatilization | DSC for T~D~ (@sec-fom); long-term ageing |
| Residue grows with sample mass | Slow decomposition during the run | Isothermal holds; NMR thermolysis at the source temperature |
| Residue ≈ %m~M~ (or the oxide or nitride), independent of mass | Decomposes before it evaporates | Not an ALD precursor at this source temperature; consider redesign or CVD |
| Two steps, first step = mass of a ligand or fragment | Ligand loss, then a new compound evaporates | Identify the off-gas (TG-MS, TG-FTIR, NMR of the condensate) |
| Step moves to higher T with larger samples, residue unchanged | Pan-area effect on evaporation | None needed |

: Reading a TGA trace for decomposition. {#tbl-tga-diagnosis}

The simulation below hands you a series of unknown precursors and a fixed amount of each. Design your own experiments, then commit to a diagnosis before the answer is revealed.

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.11: Diagnose the unknown precursor]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tgaLab = {
  // ---- Model (see Assumptions) ----
  const R = 8.314, kEff = 0.1, BUDGET = 150, ISO_MIN = 120;
  const pTorr = (s, T) => 750.06 * Math.exp(-s.H * 1000 / (R * T) + s.S / R);
  const kdec = (s, T) => (Math.LN2 / 60) * Math.exp(-s.Ea * 1000 / R * (1 / T - 1 / (s.Td + 273.15)));
  function simulate(u, m0, prog) {
    const sp = u.species, m = sp.map((_, i) => (i === 0 ? m0 : 0));
    let res = 0;
    const tot = () => 100 * (m.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) + res) / m0;
    const step = (T, dt) => {
      const mm = m.slice();
      sp.forEach((s, i) => {
        if (mm[i] <= 0) return;
        const ev = Math.min(mm[i], kEff * pTorr(s, T) * Math.sqrt(s.M / T) * dt);
        const dec = (mm[i] - ev) * (1 - Math.exp(-kdec(s, T) * dt));
        m[i] -= ev + dec;
        if (s.to === "res") res += s.y * dec; else m[s.to] += s.y * dec;
      });
    };
    const pts = [{x: prog.type === "ramp" ? 25 : 0, w: 100, d: 0}];
    if (prog.type === "ramp") {
      const dT = 0.5;
      for (let Tc = 25 + dT; Tc <= 450; Tc += dT) {
        step(Tc + 273.15, dT / prog.beta);
        const w = tot();
        pts.push({x: Tc, w, d: Math.max(0, (pts[pts.length - 1].w - w) / dT)});
      }
    } else {
      const dt = 0.25;
      for (let t = dt; t <= ISO_MIN + 1e-9; t += dt) { step(prog.T + 273.15, dt); pts.push({x: t, w: tot()}); }
    }
    const at = f => { const p = pts.find(d => d.w <= 100 - f); return p ? p.x : null; };
    return {pts, x1: at(1), x50: at(50), res: pts[pts.length - 1].w};
  }

  // ---- The unknowns (fictional compounds; parameters hidden until the reveal) ----
  const DX = {
    clean: "Clean volatilization",
    slow: "Slow decomposition during the run",
    fast: "Decomposes before it evaporates",
    step: "Stepwise conversion: loses a ligand fragment, then the product evaporates"
  };
  const UNKNOWNS = [
    {metal: "Al", M: 300, pay: 9.0, dx: "clean",
     species: [{H: 65, S: 145, M: 300, Td: 450, Ea: 150, to: "res", y: 0.09}],
     why: "One smooth step, a DTG that rises exponentially and stops abruptly, and essentially zero residue at every sample mass. A larger sample shifts the step to higher temperature only because evaporation is limited by the pan area. An isothermal run loses mass in a straight line until the pan is empty."},
    {metal: "Zr", M: 500, pay: 18.2, dx: "clean",
     species: [{H: 100, S: 160, M: 500, Td: 500, Ea: 150, to: "res", y: 0.2}],
     why: "This one is not very volatile, so it needs 200–300 °C to leave the pan, but a high temperature is not the same as decomposition. The residue stays at zero for every sample mass and ramp rate, and isothermal runs are linear. It is a clean, low-volatility precursor: the source must be hot, but the molecule survives the trip."},
    {metal: "Cu", M: 250, pay: 25.4, dx: "slow",
     species: [{H: 70, S: 150, M: 250, Td: 95, Ea: 60, to: "res", y: 0.254}],
     why: "At 10 mg the trace looks almost clean (about 2 % residue), but the residue grows with sample mass: this is the thermal stress test failing. Here decomposition has a lower activation energy than evaporation, so a slower ramp also raises the residue. An isothermal hold ends on a non-zero plateau instead of reaching zero."},
    {metal: "Ni", M: 280, pay: 21.0, dx: "slow",
     species: [{H: 70, S: 150, M: 280, Td: 110, Ea: 170, to: "res", y: 0.21}],
     why: "The 10 mg trace has under 2 % residue; at 60 mg it is over 10 %. Residue that grows with sample mass is the signature of slow decomposition. A trap: decomposition here has a higher activation energy than evaporation, so a slower ramp gives a cleaner-looking trace. Changing the ramp rate can mislead; changing the sample mass does not."},
    {metal: "Sn", M: 400, pay: 29.7, dx: "fast",
     species: [{H: 115, S: 165, M: 400, Td: 170, Ea: 130, to: "res", y: 0.297}],
     why: "The residue is about 30 % at every mass and ramp rate, which matches the tin content of the molecule: the payload stayed in the pan and the ligands left. The DTG is a rounded, nearly symmetric peak rather than a cliff, because the rate falls as the reactant is used up, not when the pan runs dry. This compound decomposes before it develops a useful vapour pressure. It might serve as a CVD precursor, but not for ALD at this source temperature."},
    {metal: "Al", M: 450, pay: 6.0, dx: "step",
     species: [{H: 100, S: 165, M: 450, Td: 115, Ea: 120, to: 1, y: 0.72},
               {H: 105, S: 160, M: 324, Td: 430, Ea: 150, to: "res", y: 0.083}],
     why: "Two steps with a flat plateau between them, and zero final residue. The first step is about 28 % of the starting mass: 126 g mol⁻¹ out of 450, exactly one iPrN=C=NiPr carbodiimide from an aluminium tris(amidinate). The product then evaporates cleanly. A zero residue does not prove a clean precursor: the molecule that reaches the reactor is not the one you loaded. An isothermal hold at 130–150 °C levels off near 70 %, the mass of the product."}
  ];

  // ---- State ----
  let order = [], cur = null, runs = [], left = BUDGET, done = false, showDTG = false;
  const shuffle = a => { for (let i = a.length - 1; i > 0; i--) { const j = Math.floor(Math.random() * (i + 1)); [a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]]; } return a; };
  const COLORS = ["#000000", "#E91C24", "#8C8C8C", "#4D4D4D", "#F08A8E", "#BFBFBF", "#7A0E12", "#2B2B2B"];
  const DASH = [null, null, null, "6,3", "6,3", "6,3", "2,2", "2,2"];

  // ---- DOM ----
  const el = (tag, attrs = {}, ...kids) => {
    const e = document.createElement(tag);
    for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(attrs)) {
      if (k === "style") e.style.cssText = v; else if (k.startsWith("on")) e.addEventListener(k.slice(2), v); else e.setAttribute(k, v);
    }
    kids.flat().forEach(k => e.append(k instanceof Node ? k : document.createTextNode(String(k))));
    return e;
  };
  const root = el("div", {class: "tga-lab"});
  const card = el("div", {class: "tga-card"});
  const controls = el("div", {class: "tga-controls"});
  const plots = el("div");
  const table = el("div");
  const verdict = el("div", {class: "tga-verdict"});

  // controls
  const typeSel = el("select", {}, el("option", {value: "ramp"}, "Ramp (10 °C min⁻¹ is standard)"), el("option", {value: "iso"}, `Isothermal hold (${ISO_MIN} min)`));
  const mass = el("input", {type: "range", min: 5, max: 80, step: 1, value: 10});
  const massOut = el("output", {}, "10 mg");
  const beta = el("input", {type: "range", min: 1, max: 20, step: 0.5, value: 10});
  const betaOut = el("output", {}, "10 °C min⁻¹");
  const Tiso = el("input", {type: "range", min: 50, max: 250, step: 5, value: 100});
  const TisoOut = el("output", {}, "100 °C");
  const runBtn = el("button", {class: "btn btn-dark btn-sm"}, "Run experiment");
  const resetBtn = el("button", {class: "btn btn-outline-dark btn-sm"}, "Reset");
  const dtgBox = el("input", {type: "checkbox"});
  const budgetOut = el("span", {class: "tga-budget"});
  const rowBeta = el("label", {class: "tga-row"}, el("span", {}, "Ramp rate"), beta, betaOut);
  const rowT = el("label", {class: "tga-row"}, el("span", {}, "Hold temperature"), Tiso, TisoOut);
  mass.oninput = () => { massOut.value = `${mass.value} mg`; syncRun(); };
  beta.oninput = () => betaOut.value = `${beta.value} °C min⁻¹`;
  Tiso.oninput = () => TisoOut.value = `${Tiso.value} °C`;
  typeSel.onchange = () => { rowBeta.style.display = typeSel.value === "ramp" ? "" : "none"; rowT.style.display = typeSel.value === "iso" ? "" : "none"; };
  rowT.style.display = "none";
  dtgBox.onchange = () => { showDTG = dtgBox.checked; drawPlots(); };
  const syncRun = () => { runBtn.disabled = done || +mass.value > left; budgetOut.textContent = `Sample left: ${left} mg of ${BUDGET}`; };
  controls.append(
    el("label", {class: "tga-row"}, el("span", {}, "Experiment"), typeSel),
    el("label", {class: "tga-row"}, el("span", {}, "Sample mass"), mass, massOut),
    rowBeta, rowT,
    el("div", {class: "tga-row"}, runBtn, resetBtn, budgetOut),
    el("label", {class: "tga-check"}, dtgBox, " Show DTG (derivative) on ramp runs")
  );

  runBtn.onclick = () => {
    const m0 = +mass.value;
    if (m0 > left || done) return;
    const prog = typeSel.value === "ramp" ? {type: "ramp", beta: +beta.value} : {type: "iso", T: +Tiso.value};
    const r = simulate(cur, m0, prog);
    left -= m0;
    runs.push({n: runs.length + 1, m0, ...prog, ...r});
    syncRun(); drawPlots(); drawTable(); drawVerdict();
  };

  function drawCard() {
    card.replaceChildren(
      el("div", {class: "tga-card-title"}, `Unknown ${UNKNOWNS.indexOf(cur) + 1} · a new ${cur.metal} precursor`),
      el("div", {}, `Molar mass ${cur.M} g mol⁻¹ · ${cur.metal} is ${cur.pay.toFixed(1)} % of the molecule by mass · you have ${BUDGET} mg to spend.`),
      el("div", {class: "tga-hint"}, "Run experiments, then commit to a diagnosis. Try to decide before you have spent all the sample.")
    );
  }

  function drawPlots() {
    const ramps = runs.filter(r => r.type === "ramp"), isos = runs.filter(r => r.type === "iso");
    const lab = r => r.pts.find(d => d.w <= 50) || r.pts[r.pts.length - 1];
    const col = r => COLORS[(r.n - 1) % COLORS.length], dash = r => DASH[(r.n - 1) % DASH.length];
    const payload = Plot.ruleY([cur.pay], {stroke: "#E91C24", strokeDasharray: "3,4", strokeOpacity: 0.7});
    const payText = (x) => Plot.text([{x, y: cur.pay}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: () => `${cur.metal} content ${cur.pay.toFixed(1)} %`, fill: "#E91C24", textAnchor: "end", dy: -7});
    const out = [];
    if (!runs.length) out.push(el("p", {class: "tga-hint"}, "No runs yet. A sensible first experiment is the standard screen: about 10 mg at 10 °C min⁻¹."));
    if (ramps.length) {
      const marks = [payload, payText(445)];
      ramps.forEach(r => {
        marks.push(Plot.line(r.pts, {x: "x", y: "w", stroke: col(r), strokeWidth: 2.2, strokeDasharray: dash(r)}));
        marks.push(Plot.text([lab(r)], {x: "x", y: "w", text: () => `#${r.n}`, fill: col(r), textAnchor: "start", dx: 6}));
        if (showDTG) {
          const dmax = d3.max(r.pts, d => d.d) || 1;
          marks.push(Plot.line(r.pts, {x: "x", y: d => 100 * d.d / dmax, stroke: col(r), strokeWidth: 1, strokeOpacity: 0.6, strokeDasharray: "2,2"}));
        }
      });
      out.push(Plot.plot({height: 330, marginLeft: 55, marginRight: 30, marginBottom: 45, marginTop: 15,
        x: {label: "Temperature (°C) →", domain: [25, 450]}, y: {label: "↑ Mass (%)", domain: [0, 105], grid: true}, marks}));
    }
    if (isos.length) {
      const marks = [payload, payText(ISO_MIN)];
      isos.forEach(r => {
        marks.push(Plot.line(r.pts, {x: "x", y: "w", stroke: col(r), strokeWidth: 2.2, strokeDasharray: dash(r)}));
        marks.push(Plot.text([lab(r)], {x: "x", y: "w", text: () => `#${r.n} (${r.T} °C)`, fill: col(r), textAnchor: "end", dy: -8}));
      });
      out.push(Plot.plot({height: 260, marginLeft: 55, marginRight: 30, marginBottom: 45, marginTop: 15,
        x: {label: "Time at temperature (min) →", domain: [0, ISO_MIN]}, y: {label: "↑ Mass (%)", domain: [0, 105], grid: true}, marks}));
    }
    plots.replaceChildren(...out);
  }

  function drawTable() {
    if (!runs.length) { table.replaceChildren(); return; }
    const f = (v, u) => v == null ? "—" : `${(+v).toFixed(u === "min" ? 1 : 0)} ${u}`;
    const rows = runs.map(r => el("tr", {},
      el("td", {}, `#${r.n}`),
      el("td", {}, r.type === "ramp" ? `ramp ${r.beta} °C min⁻¹` : `hold ${r.T} °C`),
      el("td", {}, `${r.m0} mg`),
      el("td", {}, r.type === "ramp" ? f(r.x1, "°C") : f(r.x1, "min")),
      el("td", {}, r.type === "ramp" ? f(r.x50, "°C") : f(r.x50, "min")),
      el("td", {}, `${r.res.toFixed(1)} %`)));
    table.replaceChildren(el("table", {class: "table table-sm tga-table"},
      el("thead", {}, el("tr", {}, ...["Run", "Programme", "Mass", "1 % loss", "50 % loss", "Final mass"].map(h => el("th", {}, h)))),
      el("tbody", {}, ...rows)));
  }

  function drawVerdict() {
    if (done) return;
    if (!runs.length) { verdict.replaceChildren(); return; }
    const opts = Object.entries(DX).map(([k, v]) => el("label", {class: "tga-check"}, el("input", {type: "radio", name: "tga-dx", value: k}), " ", v));
    const commit = el("button", {class: "btn btn-outline-dark btn-sm"}, "Commit diagnosis");
    commit.onclick = () => {
      const pick = verdict.querySelector("input[name=tga-dx]:checked");
      if (!pick) return;
      done = true; syncRun(); reveal(pick.value);
    };
    verdict.replaceChildren(el("div", {class: "tga-card-title"}, "Your diagnosis"), ...opts, commit);
  }

  function reveal(pick) {
    const ok = pick === cur.dx;
    const masses = new Set(runs.filter(r => r.type === "ramp").map(r => r.m0));
    const notes = [];
    if (ok && masses.size < 2 && cur.dx !== "fast" && cur.dx !== "step")
      notes.push("You got it right, but with only one sample mass you could not have ruled out slow decomposition. In practice, run the stress test before you trust a clean-looking trace.");
    if (!ok && cur.dx === "slow" && masses.size < 2)
      notes.push("The test that catches this one is the thermal stress test: repeat the ramp at a larger sample mass and compare the residues.");
    if (!ok && cur.dx === "step")
      notes.push("Look for a plateau part-way down, and compare the size of the first step with the masses of the ligands or fragments the molecule could lose.");
    if (!ok && cur.dx === "fast")
      notes.push("Compare the final mass with the metal content of the molecule: a residue that matches it, independent of sample mass, means the payload never left the pan.");
    if (!ok && cur.dx === "clean")
      notes.push("A high evaporation temperature, or a step that moves to higher temperature with a bigger sample, is not decomposition. Check whether the residue changes with sample mass.");
    const hidden = cur.species.map((sp, i) =>
      `${i ? "product" : "precursor"}: ΔHᵥₐₚ ${sp.H} kJ mol⁻¹, ΔSᵥₐₚ ${sp.S} J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, decomposition t½ = 1 h at ${sp.Td} °C, Eₐ ${sp.Ea} kJ mol⁻¹`).join("; ");
    const again = el("button", {class: "btn btn-dark btn-sm"}, "Next unknown");
    again.onclick = next;
    verdict.replaceChildren(
      el("div", {class: ok ? "tga-ok" : "tga-no"}, ok ? `Correct: ${DX[cur.dx]}.` : `Not quite. This one is: ${DX[cur.dx]}.`),
      el("p", {}, cur.why),
      ...notes.map(n => el("p", {class: "tga-hint"}, n)),
      el("p", {class: "tga-hint"}, `Hidden model: ${hidden}. Sample used: ${BUDGET - left} mg in ${runs.length} run${runs.length > 1 ? "s" : ""}.`),
      again);
  }

  // Reset: clear all runs and the diagnosis, refill the sample, keep the same unknown
  function restart() {
    runs = []; left = BUDGET; done = false;
    verdict.replaceChildren();
    drawCard(); syncRun(); drawPlots(); drawTable(); drawVerdict();
  }
  resetBtn.onclick = restart;

  function next() {
    if (!order.length) order = shuffle(UNKNOWNS.slice());
    cur = order.pop();
    restart();
  }

  root.append(card, controls, plots, table, verdict);
  next();
  return root;
}
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** Each unknown is fictional. Evaporation follows @eq-langmuir-vp from a pan of fixed area, with vapour pressure from @eq-cc (constant ΔH~vap~ and ΔS~vap~), so its rate does not depend on sample mass. Decomposition is first order in the remaining precursor with an Arrhenius rate constant; it sends a fixed fraction of the decomposed mass either to a non-volatile residue or, for one unknown, to a new compound with its own volatility. The evaporation prefactor (0.1 mg min^−1^ at 1 Torr, scaled by √(M/T)) gives traces that resemble atmospheric-pressure TGA but is not a property of any real instrument. The isothermal runs jump instantly to the hold temperature. Melting, sublimation of solids, gas-phase decomposition after evaporation, buoyancy and balance noise are ignored. The DTG of each run is scaled to the same height.

**Things to try.** Start every unknown with the standard screen (about 10 mg at 10 °C min^−1^) and decide what you expect the second run to show before you make it. Keep enough sample for a stress test at 40–60 mg. Turn on the DTG and compare a cliff with a rounded peak. When a trace has a plateau, convert the first step into g mol^−1^ (step fraction × M) and ask which fragment has that mass. For the slow decomposers, try a slower ramp as well as a bigger sample: in one of them the slower ramp hides the problem.
:::
:::

### Differential scanning calorimetry

TGA only sees decomposition that happens before or during evaporation. For a precursor that evaporates cleanly and passes the stress test, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) asks the next question: at what temperature would decomposition interfere with forming a self-limiting monolayer? [@Barry2022]

In DSC, a sample and an inert reference are heated together, and the instrument adjusts the power to each so that their temperatures stay equal. An endothermic event in the sample (melting, evaporation) needs extra power; an exothermic one (decomposition) needs less. Plotted against temperature, endotherms are usually drawn downward and exotherms upward. For precursor testing, the pan must be **sealed without a pinhole**: if the sample can escape, the DSC only repeats what the TGA has already said [@Barry2022].

A typical trace might show an endotherm at 150 °C (melting) and a strong exotherm at 270 °C (probably decomposition). Running the sample through the same temperature range twice separates the two: melting comes back on the second cycle, decomposition does not. The exotherm onset is a reasonable working value for T~D~, though it should be confirmed by an independent test at that temperature [@Barry2022].

### Thermal range and figure of merit {#sec-fom}

T~V~ and T~D~ bracket the thermal range in which an ALD process can be sought: hot enough to deliver vapour, cool enough that the precursor neither decomposes into the film nor deposits continuously. To rank large families of candidates, a single number helps [@Barry2022]:

$$
\sigma = (T_\text{D} - T_\text{V})\left(1 - \frac{\%m_\text{r}}{\%m_\text{M}}\right)
$$ {#eq-fom}

Here %m~r~ is the TGA residual mass and %m~M~ the mass percentage of the payload atom in the precursor. The second factor estimates how much of the payload failed to volatilize, and shrinks the thermal range accordingly [@Barry2022].

σ is a ranking tool, not a verdict. It can go negative in two ways: T~V~ above T~D~ (the compound decomposes before it evaporates, so it is a poor ALD precursor, though it might work for CVD), or a residue larger than the payload alone can explain. If **both** terms are negative, σ comes out positive for a truly terrible precursor [@Barry2022]. Use it to compare candidates that already look reasonable, and look at the data behind the number.

### Decomposition testing {#sec-decomposition-testing}

Thermal testing can also diagnose *how* a precursor decomposes, which is what a redesign needs. A simple method is to seal the precursor in solution in an NMR tube, keep it in an oven at the temperature of interest, and record spectra over time [@Barry2022]. The half-lives in Simulation 2.10 come from experiments of this kind.

Solution is a different thermodynamic system from the condensed precursor and from the gas phase, so it can highlight the wrong pathway. The gold guanidinates are the cautionary example [@Barry2022]. In solution, they decompose by carbodiimide deinsertion, and the carbodiimide can be isolated to prove it. In a modified ALD reactor in which the gaseous by-products were collected, carbodiimide was only a minor product at 150 °C. The main route was β-hydrogen abstraction, releasing an "oxidized guanidinate"; the gold hydride left behind immediately gave gold metal. Both pathways are open at 150 °C, but the β-H route is faster at a surface. Measure thermolysis under conditions as close to the process as you can.

#### Recognizing decomposition

When a precursor decomposes instead of reacting cleanly, growth gains a **CVD component**. Signs include:

- GPC that keeps rising with dose, or rises sharply with temperature above the ALD window
- A thickness gradient along the gas-flow direction
- Carbon or nitrogen in the film, or a large residue in TGA

Decomposition can also happen in the **source**, long before the precursor reaches the substrate, and a fast TGA ramp does not test days at source temperature. When TTIP was held in a sealed container at 120, 150 or 180 °C for 7 days, its decomposition products changed its vapour pressure and its TGA behaviour. TiO~2~ films grown from the stressed precursor had a different growth rate, poorer uniformity (after stress at 180 °C), more Ti^2+^ and higher leakage current [@Kim2022]. Decomposition is not always unwanted, though. It can be used deliberately, for example by adsorbing a precursor self-limitingly at low temperature and then decomposing it in a separate heating step.

### Volatility control {#sec-volatility-control}

A liquid is often more volatile than a solid, since its molecules are on average farther apart, and melting-point control (@sec-designing-precursors) can help. That rule holds for closely related molecules and fails across families, so volatility is mostly improved by trial and error [@Barry2022].

One ploy that works reliably is to **reduce the ability to bridge**. Group 13 compounds with group 15 donor ligands (the precursors for III–V semiconductors) are prone to oligomerize through the lone pair on N, P or As. In a family of gallium compounds with a chelating ethylenediamide ligand, RN–CH~2~CH~2~–NMe~2~, the compound with R = methyl exists in solution as a monomer–dimer equilibrium, because the small R group lets the ligand of one molecule reach the gallium of the next. With R = ethyl, it is monomeric [@Barry2022]. Fewer intermolecular bonds, lower ΔH~vap~, higher vapour pressure. TMA and DMAI (@sec-tma-dmai) show the same effect in reverse.

The two calculators below turn vapour-pressure data into the numbers a process needs.

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.12: Vapour pressure and source temperature]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof dHvap = Inputs.range([30, 160], {value: 70, step: 1, label: "ΔHᵥₐₚ (kJ mol⁻¹)"})
viewof dSvap = Inputs.range([60, 250], {value: 150, step: 1, label: "ΔSᵥₐₚ (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)"})
viewof pTarget = Inputs.select([0.1, 0.5, 1, 5], {value: 1, label: "Target vapour pressure (Torr)", format: x => `${x} Torr`})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
vp = {
  const R = 8.314, p0 = 750.06;                    // Torr per bar
  const p = T => p0 * Math.exp(-dHvap * 1000 / (R * T) + dSvap / R);
  const Tt = dHvap * 1000 / (dSvap - R * Math.log(pTarget / p0));   // K at target p
  const Tb = dHvap * 1000 / dSvap;                                  // K at 1 bar
  const pts = d3.range(250, 673.2, 2).map(T => ({T: T - 273.15, p: p(T)}));
  return {Tt, Tb, pts, p25: p(298.15)};
}

Plot.plot({
  height: 340, marginLeft: 70, marginBottom: 50, marginTop: 20,
  x: {label: "Temperature (°C) →", domain: [-25, 400]},
  y: {label: "↑ Vapour pressure (Torr)", type: "log", domain: [1e-4, 1e4], grid: true, tickFormat: "~g"},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY([{}], {x1: -25, x2: 400, y1: 0.1, y2: 1, fill: "#E91C24", fillOpacity: 0.07}),
    Plot.ruleY([pTarget], {stroke: "#E91C24", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(vp.pts.filter(d => d.p > 1e-4 && d.p < 1e4), {x: "T", y: "p", stroke: "#000", strokeWidth: 2, clip: true}),
    Plot.dot([{T: vp.Tt - 273.15, p: pTarget}], {x: "T", y: "p", r: 6, fill: "#E91C24"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Temperature for **${pTarget} Torr**: **${(vp.Tt - 273.15).toFixed(0)} °C** · Vapour pressure at 25 °C: **${vp.p25 < 0.01 ? vp.p25.toExponential(1) : vp.p25.toFixed(2)} Torr** · Normal boiling (or sublimation) point: **${(vp.Tb - 273.15).toFixed(0)} °C**`
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** ΔH~vap~ and ΔS~vap~ are constant with temperature, and the vapour is ideal. The shaded band (0.1–1 Torr) is a common working range for ALD sources. For many liquids, ΔS~vap~ at the boiling point is close to Trouton's value of about 85–90 J K^−1^ mol^−1^; associated liquids and many solids (where ΔH includes the enthalpy of fusion) depart from it. The model does not account for decomposition: a compound may decompose before it reaches the temperature shown.
:::
:::

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.13: Vapour pressure from a stepped isotherm]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof siData = Inputs.textarea({label: "T (°C), Δm/Δt (µg min⁻¹)", rows: 9, width: 260,
  value: "45, 6.7\n50, 9.6\n55, 14.0\n60, 19.6\n65, 27.4\n70, 38.8\n75, 55.1\n80, 74.7"})
viewof siCalT = Inputs.number({value: 60, label: "Calibration: at T (°C)"})
viewof siCalP = Inputs.number({value: 0.5, label: "the vapour pressure is (Torr)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
si = {
  const R = 8.314;
  const pts = siData.split(/\n/).map(l => l.split(/[,;\s\t]+/).filter(Boolean).map(Number))
    .filter(a => a.length >= 2 && isFinite(a[0]) && isFinite(a[1]) && a[1] > 0)
    .map(([t, r]) => ({t, T: t + 273.15, x: 1 / (t + 273.15), y: Math.log(r * Math.sqrt(t + 273.15))}));
  if (pts.length < 2) return {ok: false};
  const n = pts.length, mx = d3.mean(pts, d => d.x), my = d3.mean(pts, d => d.y);
  const sxy = d3.sum(pts, d => (d.x - mx) * (d.y - my)), sxx = d3.sum(pts, d => (d.x - mx) ** 2);
  const slope = sxy / sxx, icpt = my - slope * mx;
  const syy = d3.sum(pts, d => (d.y - my) ** 2), r2 = sxy * sxy / (sxx * syy);
  const dH = -slope * R / 1000;                                  // kJ mol⁻¹
  // absolute scale from the calibration point: ln p = ln p_cal - ΔH/R (1/T - 1/T_cal)
  const Tc = siCalT + 273.15;
  const lnp = T => Math.log(siCalP) - dH * 1000 / R * (1 / T - 1 / Tc);
  const Tv = 1 / (1 / Tc + R * Math.log(siCalP) / (dH * 1000)) - 273.15;
  const fit = d3.range(0, 41).map(i => { const x = d3.min(pts, d => d.x) + (d3.max(pts, d => d.x) - d3.min(pts, d => d.x)) * i / 40; return {x, y: icpt + slope * x}; });
  return {ok: true, pts, fit, dH, r2, Tv, lnp, n};
}

si.ok ? Plot.plot({
  height: 300, marginLeft: 70, marginBottom: 50, marginTop: 20,
  x: {label: "1000 / T (K⁻¹) →", transform: x => 1000 * x},
  y: {label: "↑ ln[(Δm/Δt)·√T]", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(si.fit, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#8C8C8C", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.dot(si.pts, {x: "x", y: "y", r: 5, fill: "#E91C24", stroke: "#000", tip: true, channels: {"T (°C)": "t"}})
  ]
}) : md`*Enter at least two lines of the form* \`T, rate\`.`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
si.ok ? md`From ${si.n} points: ΔH_vap = **${si.dH.toFixed(1)} kJ mol⁻¹** (R² = ${si.r2.toFixed(4)}). With the calibration point, T_V (1 Torr) = **${si.Tv.toFixed(0)} °C**; vapour pressure at the hottest step = **${Math.exp(si.lnp(d3.max(si.pts, d => d.T))).toPrecision(3)} Torr**.` : md``
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** @eq-langmuir-vp with a constant prefactor, so ln[(Δm/Δt)√T] is linear in 1/T with slope −ΔH~vap~/R, whatever the (unknown) calibration constant; the molar mass cancels from the slope. ΔH~vap~ is assumed constant over the range. The calibration point sets the absolute scale and is needed only for T~V~; in practice it comes from a reference compound measured in the same instrument. The default data are synthetic (ΔH~vap~ = 65 kJ mol^−1^ with 3 % noise). Paste your own data to analyse it.
:::
:::

### Impurity control

A common source of film impurities is the atom bonded directly to the metal in the precursor. Those bonds have to be strong to survive volatilization, and they are often the ones that survive into the film [@Barry2022]. AlN is the clearest example. From TMA and ammonia, films typically contain 10–15 at. % carbon, depending on temperature, because every Al starts with three Al–C bonds. Dihydridodimethylamidoaluminum(III), with Al–H and Al–N bonds but no Al–C bonds, gives AlN with less than 1 at. % carbon, below the detection limit of common film analysis [@Barry2022]. Impurity is not the only difference between the two precursors, but the design logic is general: **if an element must stay out of the film, keep it off the metal.**

### When self-limiting becomes CVD: Au at 120 °C {#sec-au-120}

Trimethyl(trimethylphosphine)gold(III), Me~3~AuPMe~3~, is a liquid, air- and water-stable precursor that gave the first ALD process for pure gold [@Griffiths2016]. Its story shows how a process can look self-limiting and still have a decomposition problem hiding at the top of its temperature range.

- **The first process (120 °C).** An oxygen plasma converts the precursor to gold, but combustion of the phosphine leaves phosphorus oxide in the film. Adding a water pulse after the plasma hydrolyses it to phosphoric acid, which is purged away. The resulting three-step process gave pure metallic gold with a self-limiting GPC of 0.5 Å [@Griffiths2016].
- **A second process (50–120 °C).** With an H~2~ plasma as the second precursor, the GPC was 0.30 Å, again with clear saturation, and films grown at 120 °C were very pure (< 1 at. % C and O, < 0.1 at. % P) [@VanDaele2019].
- **The mechanism.** In situ infrared spectroscopy, in vacuo XPS and mass spectrometry showed that both methyl and PMe~3~ ligands stay on the gold surface after the precursor pulse, and the H~2~ plasma removes both [@VanDaele2020]. Above 100 °C, however, the surface ligands begin to desorb *during* the precursor exposure. Each ligand that leaves frees a site for more precursor, so growth is no longer limited by the surface: it becomes decomposition-driven, CVD-like growth. The safe upper limit of the process was revised from 120 °C down to 100 °C [@VanDaele2020]. On bare SiO~2~, by contrast, the precursor did not decompose.

Three lessons carry over to every process:

1. **Self-limitation depends on how long the ligands stay, not only on how fast the precursor reacts.** Here the residence time of the surface ligands (@eq-residence) fell below the length of the pulse. A saturation curve recorded with short pulses can look flat while slow ligand loss adds growth at longer exposures.
2. **The surface is a reactant.** Gold catalyses ligand loss that does not happen on silica or in the source, so T~D~ from TGA or DSC cannot predict it. Decomposition at the substrate has to be tested at the substrate.
3. **Mechanism studies change process windows.** A window reported from GPC data alone moved by 20 °C once the surface chemistry was followed directly. The same precursor also shows the association and dissociation steps discussed next (@sec-assoc-dissoc), and the island growth of @sec-nucleation-energetics.

## Surface reaction mechanisms {#sec-mechanisms}

[Applies to: ALD · MLD · ALE · ASD]{.applies}

Surface reactions are often described with a handful of labels: ligand exchange, dissociation, association, combustion [@Richey2020]. Careful studies regularly find that the real path is messier, with several steps and more than one route competing, and that the classic one-step ligand exchange does not describe it well [@Richey2020]. A more useful approach is to treat the surface as one more ligand on the metal, and to borrow the reaction steps of organometallic chemistry. These steps come in pairs, each the reverse of the other [@Barry2022]:

| Step | Idealized reaction | Effect on the metal's oxidation state |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Association | ML~n~ + L → ML~n+1~ | None |
| Dissociation | ML~n+1~ → ML~n~ + L | None |
| Comproportionation | M^(n−x)+^ + M^(n+x)+^ → 2 M^n+^ | One decreases, one increases |
| Disproportionation | 2 M^n+^ → M^(n−x)+^ + M^(n+x)+^ | One increases, one decreases |
| Oxidative addition | ML~n~ + X~2~ → ML~n~X~2~ | Increases by 2 |
| Reductive elimination | ML~n~X~2~ → ML~n~ + X~2~ | Decreases by 2 |
| Migratory insertion | ML~n~X → ML~n−1~(X–L) | None |
| β-Elimination | ML~n−1~(X–L) → ML~n~X | None |

: The fundamental reaction steps of inorganic and organometallic chemistry [@Barry2022]. {#tbl-mechanism-steps}

Ligand exchange, the most common surface reaction of all, is a combination of these steps (association then dissociation, or the reverse). The examples below are taken from Chapter 7 of @Barry2022.

### Reaction with surface hydroxyls {#sec-hydroxyl-reaction}

The archetypal surface reaction is the Brønsted acid–base reaction of a metal precursor with a surface hydroxyl (@eq-acidbase). For TMA, allowing for the fact that it reacts with either one or two –OH groups, the two half-reactions can be written [@Barry2022]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3\,\|\!-\!\text{OH} + 2\,\text{AlMe}_3 &\rightarrow \|\!-\!\text{OAlMe}_2 + (\|\!-\!\text{O})_2\text{AlMe} + 3\,\text{CH}_4 \\
\|\!-\!\text{OAlMe}_2 + (\|\!-\!\text{O})_2\text{AlMe} + 3\,\text{H}_2\text{O} &\rightarrow 3\,\|\!-\!\text{OH} + 3\,\text{CH}_4
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-tma-stoich}

Hydroxylated surfaces also dehydrate as the temperature rises, 2 ‖–OH → ‖–O–‖ + H~2~O, which is why the GPC of TMA/H~2~O falls at higher temperature [@Barry2022].

The single arrow hides at least two steps. The likely path starts with an association: a lone pair on the surface oxygen donates into the empty p orbital on aluminum, making a Lewis acid–base adduct. A proton then moves from the –OH to a methyl group, which leaves as methane [@Barry2021]. Two general rules follow: strongly Lewis-acidic metals adsorb readily, and more basic leaving ligands (alkyl > amide > alkoxide) are protonated faster (@tbl-pka). Neighbouring adsorbates also matter. Computational work shows that nearby fragments assist proton transfer and ligand loss, and that the reaction stops partly because the surface metal atoms become fully coordinated, not only because the hydroxyls run out [@Shirazi2015].

### Association and dissociation {#sec-assoc-dissoc}

Every atomic layer process starts with an **association**: the physisorption of a precursor, or of a fragment of one, at the surface [@Barry2022]. AlCl~3~ shows the two possible outcomes (@sec-precursors). Physisorbed through a dative bond from a surface oxygen, it can easily leave again. Chemisorbed by losing a chloride, it cannot.

Chemisorption does not always need a reaction with a surface site. Mo(CO)~6~ coordinates to an aluminum atom in an alumina surface at room temperature, bridging through one of its carbonyls, and then **dissociates** a CO ligand. Once the CO is pumped away, the fragment has no easy way to leave: losing a ligand into the gas, in a separate step, is enough to make the adsorption irreversible [@Barry2022].

Dissociation at a surface can also cause trouble. Me~3~AuPMe~3~ on gold splits into two surface species [@Barry2022]:

$$
\|\!-\!\text{Au} + \|\!-\!\text{Au} + \text{Me}_3\text{AuPMe}_3 \rightarrow \|\!-\!\text{AuMe}_3 + \|\!-\!\text{Au–PMe}_3
$$

A ligand that binds strongly to the surface takes up sites that the precursor needs, and if it decomposes, it leaves impurities. With an oxygen plasma alone, the phosphine burns to P~2~O~5~, which stays in the film until a water pulse converts it to volatile phosphoric acid, P~2~O~5~ + 3 H~2~O → 2 H~3~PO~4~ [@Barry2022; @Griffiths2016]. With an H~2~ plasma, the methyls leave as methane and the phosphine is broken down to methane and smaller phosphines [@Barry2022]. Ligand exchange itself can be fully associative (the new ligand binds before the old one leaves), fully dissociative (the reverse order), or in between [@Barry2022].

### Reductive elimination and oxidative addition {#sec-reductive-elimination}

When the metal's oxidation state in the film differs from that in the precursor, something must transfer electrons. **Reductive elimination** does this by joining two ligands into a stable molecule and reducing the metal by two electrons.

TiN is the standard example. Ti(IV) precursors are preferred because they are more stable than Ti(III) ones, but TiN contains Ti(III). For TiCl~4~ and NH~3~, the overall reaction is usually written TiCl~4~ + 2 NH~3~ → TiN + 4 HCl + H~2~ + ½ N~2~ [@Barry2022]. Reductive elimination at the surface can account for both gases [@Barry2022]:

- **N~2~**: 2 ‖–Ti~3~N~4~ → 2 ‖–Ti~3~N~3~ + N~2~, reducing Ti(IV) to Ti(III) while oxidizing N^3−^ to N^0^.
- **H~2~**: a surface amide gives up a hydrogen to a neighbouring titanium, ‖–Ti–NH~2~ + ‖–Ti → ‖–Ti=NH + ‖–Ti–H, and two surface hydrides then eliminate H~2~.

Stronger evidence comes from TiN grown from Ti(NMeEt)~4~ and NH~3~, where a chemisorbed imine and the free amine are both observed [@Barry2022]. An alternative explanation for amide precursors is β-hydrogen elimination to a surface imine, giving a formal Ti(II) that comproportionates with neighbouring Ti(IV) [@Barry2021].

A precursor cannot carry two ligands that could reductively eliminate from it, because it would then decompose continuously, which is CVD. In copper ALD the step is set up *after* chemisorption [@Barry2022]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\,\|\!-\!\text{Cu(dmae)} + \text{ZnEt}_2 &\rightarrow 2\,\|\!-\!\text{CuEt} + \text{Zn(dmae)}_2 \\
2\,\|\!-\!\text{CuEt} &\rightarrow 2\,\|\!-\!\text{Cu}^0 + \text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}
\end{aligned}
$$

The surface Cu(dmae) groups come from Cu(dmae)~2~ (dmae = dimethylaminoethoxide), which loses one ligand to a copper surface; see comproportionation below. With H~2~ instead of ZnEt~2~, the same surface groups form a copper hydride that eliminates H~2~. A simpler reduction, with no elimination, uses zinc vapour: 2 ‖–CuCl + Zn → 2 ‖–Cu + ZnCl~2~ [@Barry2022].

**Oxidative addition**, the reverse step, raises the oxidation state. SnO~2~ can be grown from a tin(II) N-heterocyclic stannylene and hydrogen peroxide. The stannylene first binds two surface hydroxyls and releases its ligand as the diamine. H~2~O~2~ then adds across the surface tin, breaking its O–O bond and oxidizing Sn(II) to Sn(IV), which leaves a surface tin with two hydroxyl groups ready for the next cycle [@Barry2022].

### Migratory insertion and β-elimination {#sec-migratory-insertion}

In **migratory insertion**, a ligand moves from the metal onto a neighbouring atom. TMA and ozone show it at work [@Barry2022; @Goldstein2008]:

1. TMA chemisorbs on –OH as usual.
2. Ozone, or an oxygen atom from it, coordinates to aluminum, and a methyl migrates onto the oxygen. The result looks like an insertion of O into the Al–C bond, giving a surface methoxy group. O can insert into C–H bonds the same way.
3. Neighbouring methoxy groups and further oxygen give formate and bicarbonate groups, which lose CO or CO~2~ and leave surface –OH.
4. Once –OH groups exist again, TMA can chemisorb by the ordinary acid–base route, which is why the TMA/O~3~ process has a similar temperature dependence to TMA/H~2~O. Ethene, seen early in the ozone pulse, probably comes from a minor route in which CH~2~ fragments couple.

**β-Elimination** is the reverse step, and the most common way for a precursor to decompose (@sec-designing-precursors). A surface Cu(dmae) group, for example, undergoes β-hydrogen elimination if the surface is hot enough, forming a copper hydride that reductively eliminates. That route is not self-limiting, so Cu(dmae)~2~ gives ALD at low temperature and CVD at high temperature [@Barry2022].

### Disproportionation and comproportionation

Copper shows both. When Cu(dmae)~2~ meets a copper surface, it loses a ligand to the surface, and the Cu(II) adatom **comproportionates** with a surface Cu(0) to give two Cu(I) centres, ‖–Cu^0^ + ‖–Cu^2+^ → 2 ‖–Cu^+^ [@Barry2022]. Cu(I) compounds can also **disproportionate**, 2 CuL → Cu^0^ + CuL~2~. Because this reaction does not stop, it is fatal to ALD; it is also why copper(I) β-diketonates make excellent CVD precursors. Nitrogen-based ligands suppress it [@Barry2022].

### Ligand exchange {#sec-ligand-exchange}

Ligand exchange swaps a ligand on the metal for a group from somewhere else: a proton from a surface –OH (protonolysis, @sec-hydroxyl-reaction), an alkyl from a second metal precursor (the ZnEt~2~ step above), or a hydride from the surface (@sec-hydride-surfaces). Two ideas from earlier in the chapter decide which exchange happens. The basicity of the leaving ligand sets a first guess (@tbl-pka), and the fact that products are swept away means that ALD surface reactions are never at equilibrium, so less favourable exchanges can compete [@Barry2021].

The same reaction runs in the other direction in **thermal ALE**. There, a fluorination step converts the top of an Al~2~O~3~ film to AlF~3~, and a precursor such as Sn(acac)~2~ then exchanges its acac ligands for fluoride, taking aluminum away as a volatile complex [@Lee2015; @George2016]. The requirements are the ones in @sec-precursors read backwards: the *product* of the exchange must be volatile and thermally stable, and the reaction must stop once the modified layer is used up. The ALE chapter (in preparation) develops this in detail.

## Surfaces and nucleation sites {#sec-surfaces}

[Applies to: ALD · MLD · ASD]{.applies}

The surface is half of every reaction in this chapter, and it changes during a process: first the substrate, then the growing film (@sec-vocabulary). Chapter 6 of @Barry2022 classifies surfaces by the nucleation sites they offer. This section follows that classification, then looks at what happens when sites are scarce.

### Protonated surfaces {#sec-protonated-surfaces}

Hydroxyls are the most-taught nucleation sites, for good reason: they terminate the native oxide on silicon, and SiO~2~ and Al~2~O~3~, which are the most common starting and growing surfaces [@Barry2022]. Any oxide exposed to water carries –OH groups, and so does an oxophilic metal that has oxidized in air. A nitride exposed to ammonia carries –NH and –NH~2~ groups instead, with two different pK~a~ values and so two different reactivities [@Barry2022].

Not all hydroxyl surfaces are equal. At 350 °C, silica carries about 3.5 OH nm^−2^, mostly isolated single hydroxyls (about 100 for every 6 geminal pairs), so its reactivity is relatively uniform. Alumina carries 5–7 OH nm^−2^ at the same temperature, spread over five distinct environments on tetrahedral and octahedral aluminum, in proportions that depend on how the surface was prepared [@Barry2022]. Hydroxyl density falls as the surface dehydrates; silica can be stripped of hydroxyls completely at about 900 °C. Pre-heating a substrate is therefore a way to tune the first cycles of a process [@Barry2022].

Density changes chemistry, not just GPC. A titanium precursor carrying both Cp and guanidinate ligands keeps one of each when it chemisorbs on silica pre-treated at low temperature, because a neighbouring –OH hydrogen-bonds to the guanidinate and holds it in place. On silica pre-treated at high temperature, with fewer neighbours, it loses its guanidinates instead and keeps its Cp ligands [@Barry2022].

### Metal surfaces {#sec-metal-surfaces}

A clean metal surface offers a different set of sites: single atoms on a terrace, atoms on flat and stepped edges, bridges between two atoms on a terrace or an edge, and three-fold hollows between three atoms [@Barry2022]. These sites are more alike than the hydroxyls on an oxide, but metals are also *less* selective about what they bind. A precursor can bond through its ligands as well as through its metal. Bis(dimethylamino-2-propoxo)copper(II) adsorbs on Cu(111) at several kinds of site, but always through both the copper and the ligand oxygens, a hint that the growing film could pick up oxygen [@Barry2022]. Metal surfaces can also catalyse ligand loss, as the gold example in @sec-au-120 showed.

### Hydride surfaces {#sec-hydride-surfaces}

In inorganic chemistry, hydrogen bonded to a less electronegative element (χ < 2.20) is a hydride, H^δ−^. By that definition most hydrogen-terminated metal surfaces (χ from about 0.7 to 2.16) are hydride surfaces, and the larger the electronegativity difference, the more hydridic the hydrogen: Ti–H (Δχ = 0.66) is much more active than Mo–H (Δχ = 0.04). H-terminated silicon (Δχ = 0.30) is also a hydride surface. The noble metals (Ru, Rh, Pd, Os, Ir, Pt, Au, χ = 2.20–2.54), W and Pb polarize the bond the other way, and their surface hydrogens behave as protons, so ordinary Brønsted chemistry is the right first guess there [@Barry2022].

On a hydride surface, the reaction to consider is with H^−^. TMA on Si–H has two options [@Barry2022]:

- **Exchange** of CH~3~^−^ and H^−^ between Si and Al, with no net stabilization. Viable, but with no driving force, so methyl saturation would be slow.
- **Elimination of methane**, with a net stabilization of about 40 kJ mol^−1^. The surface hydride combines with a methyl to give CH~4~, in which the hydrogen is now protic because carbon (χ = 2.55) is more electronegative than hydrogen. Formally, this is a redox reaction: the hydride is oxidized and the surface silicon reduced.

### Nucleation energetics: clean versus defect-rich surfaces {#sec-nucleation-energetics}

Growth needs nuclei, and nuclei need sites. On a surface rich in the right groups, every site is a potential nucleus and growth is linear from the first cycle. On a surface that lacks them (H-terminated silicon for a precursor that needs –OH, or an oxide for a metal that binds it weakly), the first nuclei can only form at **defects**: residual hydroxyls, step edges, impurities, vacancies.

Classical nucleation theory makes this quantitative. A small cluster of the film on a substrate costs surface energy and gains bulk free energy, so its free energy passes through a maximum, ΔG\*, at a critical size. On a substrate, the barrier is reduced by a wetting factor that depends on the contact angle θ between film and substrate:

$$
\Delta G^*_\text{het} = \Delta G^*_\text{hom}\, f(\theta), \qquad f(\theta) = \frac{(2+\cos\theta)(1-\cos\theta)^2}{4}
$$ {#eq-cnt}

A film that wets the substrate (small θ) nucleates easily and can grow layer by layer. A film that interacts weakly (θ large, f → 1) forms islands: the Volmer–Weber growth of metals on oxides. Gold from Me~3~AuPMe~3~ forms discrete nanoparticles after 2–5 cycles rather than a continuous film [@Griffiths2016], and with an H~2~ plasma the particles grow and coalesce into worm-like nanostructures [@VanDaele2019]. A defect lowers ΔG\* locally. Because the nucleation rate depends exponentially on the barrier, J ∝ exp(−ΔG\*/k~B~T), a few kJ mol^−1^ makes a defect many times more likely to nucleate than a terrace site. On a clean surface with few defects, nucleation is slow and sparse; on a defect-rich one, it is fast and dense.

This is why selectivity in deposition is best described by *relative nucleation rates* on different surfaces [@Gladfelter1993], and it is the physical basis of inherent area-selective deposition: a long nucleation delay on the non-growth surface and none on the growth surface give a window of cycles in which film grows only where it is wanted (@sec-history-asd).

### Initial growth and growth modes {#sec-growth-modes}

The first cycles on a new substrate rarely look like the steady state. The substrate's own surface chemistry sets how many reactive sites are available at first. Puurunen and Vandervorst classified the behaviour as **linear**, **substrate-enhanced** or **substrate-inhibited** growth, and further divided substrate-inhibited growth into two types, the second of which involves island growth [@Puurunen2004].

A simple way to capture the first three cases is a GPC that relaxes exponentially from an initial value $r\,\mathrm{GPC}_\infty$ to the steady-state value $\mathrm{GPC}_\infty$ over a characteristic number of cycles $n_0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{GPC}(n) &= \mathrm{GPC}_\infty\left[1 + (r-1)\,e^{-n/n_0}\right] \\
d(N) &= \mathrm{GPC}_\infty\left[N + (r-1)\,n_0\left(1-e^{-N/n_0}\right)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-nucleation}

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.14: Thickness versus cycles with a nucleation transient]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rInit = Inputs.range([0, 3], {value: 0.2, step: 0.05, label: "Initial GPC / steady-state GPC, r"})
viewof nTrans = Inputs.range([1, 100], {value: 20, step: 1, label: "Transient length, n₀ (cycles)"})
viewof gpcInf = Inputs.range([0.2, 2], {value: 1.0, step: 0.05, label: "Steady-state GPC (Å)"})
viewof nCycles = Inputs.range([10, 500], {value: 100, step: 5, label: "Cycles deposited, N"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
nuc = {
  const d = n => gpcInf * (n + (rInit - 1) * nTrans * (1 - Math.exp(-n / nTrans)));
  const pts = d3.range(0, nCycles + 1).map(n => ({n, d: d(n)}));
  const offset = (rInit - 1) * nTrans;          // asymptote: d = GPC∞ (n + offset)
  const asym = [{n: Math.max(0, -offset), d: Math.max(0, gpcInf * offset)}, {n: nCycles, d: gpcInf * (nCycles + offset)}];
  return {pts, asym, offset, dN: d(nCycles), apparent: d(nCycles) / nCycles};
}

Plot.plot({
  height: 340, marginLeft: 65, marginBottom: 50, marginTop: 30,
  x: {label: "Cycle number →"},
  y: {label: "↑ Thickness (Å)", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(nuc.asym, {x: "n", y: "d", stroke: "#8C8C8C", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(nuc.pts.map(p => ({n: p.n, d: gpcInf * p.n})), {x: "n", y: "d", stroke: "#BFBFBF"}),
    Plot.line(nuc.pts, {x: "n", y: "d", stroke: "#000000", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot([{n: nCycles, d: nuc.dN}], {x: "n", y: "d", r: 5, fill: "#E91C24"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Thickness after ${nCycles} cycles: **${nuc.dN.toFixed(1)} Å** · Apparent GPC (d/N): **${nuc.apparent.toFixed(3)} Å** vs. true steady state **${gpcInf.toFixed(2)} Å** (${(100 * (nuc.apparent / gpcInf - 1)).toFixed(1)} % error)

${nuc.offset < 0 ? `Extrapolated nucleation delay (dashed line intercept): **${(-nuc.offset).toFixed(1)} cycles**` : `Extrapolated thickness offset: **+${(gpcInf * nuc.offset).toFixed(1)} Å** (substrate-enhanced)`}`
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions:** smooth, laterally uniform growth; a single exponential transient. This model does **not** reproduce the GPC overshoot of island growth (substrate-inhibited type 2), and it treats the film as continuous from the first cycle, which is false for strongly inhibited nucleation. Grey line: ideal linear growth. Dashed line: steady-state asymptote.
:::
:::

The practical lesson is that **a single thickness divided by a single cycle count is a biased GPC estimate.** Measure several cycle numbers and take the slope of the linear part instead. The bias is largest for thin films, which are exactly the films where ALD is usually chosen.

## Check your understanding

### Saturation and surface kinetics

::: {.quiz}
A colleague fits a measured plot of GPC against TMA pulse time to the Langmuir isotherm, θ = Kp/(1 + Kp). What is wrong with this?

- [ ] Nothing; the Langmuir isotherm is the saturation curve.
- [x] The isotherm gives the equilibrium coverage as a function of pressure at infinite time. A pulse series at fixed pressure follows the time-dependent solution, θ(t) = θ~eq~[1 − exp(−(k~a~p + k~d~)t)].
- [ ] The isotherm only applies to physisorption.
- [ ] GPC cannot be related to coverage.

::: {.explanation}
The two come from the same rate equations (@eq-rates) but answer different questions. The isotherm is the plateau that the saturation curve approaches; the saturation curve describes how it gets there [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A precursor physisorbs with an adsorption energy of about 40 kJ mol^−1^. Why can this step alone not make a self-limiting ALD half-reaction at 200 °C?

- [ ] Physisorption is always slower than chemisorption.
- [x] Its residence time (@eq-residence) is of the order of nanoseconds, so the layer desorbs as soon as the gas-phase pressure drops during the purge.
- [ ] Physisorbed molecules cannot be removed by the next precursor.
- [ ] Physisorption only occurs below room temperature.

::: {.explanation}
τ = τ~0~ exp(E~des~/RT) ≈ 10^−13^ s × exp(10) ≈ a few ns. A self-limiting step needs the adsorbed layer to outlast the purge, which in practice means chemisorption, usually with loss of a ligand [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A metal ALD process gives a well-defined plateau at a GPC of 0.3 Å, far below the thickness of a monolayer of the metal. A student concludes that the precursor dose is too small. What is the best response?

- [ ] Correct; any plateau below one monolayer means undersaturation.
- [x] A plateau is saturation. If desorption competes with adsorption (k~d~ > 0), the plateau sits at θ~eq~ < 1; steric bulk and site density can also cap it. More dose will not raise it.
- [ ] The second precursor must be in excess.
- [ ] The plateau must be an artefact of the thickness measurement.

::: {.explanation}
@eq-saturation reaches a plateau at θ~eq~ = k~a~p/(k~a~p + k~d~), which is below 1 whenever k~d~ is not negligible. This is one reason metal processes often have low GPCs [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Why is the TMA/H~2~O growth per cycle well below one monolayer of Al~2~O~3~?

- [ ] Purges are never complete, so some material is removed every cycle.
