- [ ] The water step partially etches the film.
- [x] Steric hindrance from the remaining methyl ligands, and the limited number of reactive surface sites, cap how much Al can adsorb per cycle.
- [ ] As-deposited ALD alumina is highly porous.

::: {.explanation}
The GPC is set by how many precursor molecules fit and react on the surface in one half-cycle. Ligand size (steric hindrance) and site density are the two limiting factors [@Puurunen2005].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A colleague claims a process is "true ALD" because its GPC is constant between 150 and 250 °C. What is wrong with this argument?

- [ ] Nothing; a flat window is the standard proof of ALD.
- [x] A plateau in temperature neither proves nor is required for self-limitation; only dose and purge saturation tests establish it.
- [ ] The window must span at least 200 °C.
- [ ] GPC must increase with temperature in a true ALD process.

::: {.explanation}
Self-limiting processes can have temperature-dependent GPC (TMA/H~2~O is the standard example). A flat region can also arise from competing non-ideal effects. Saturation is tested in dose, not in temperature.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A 50-cycle film is 3.0 nm thick. The steady-state GPC is known to be 1.0 Å. Assuming growth is linear after an abrupt nucleation delay, how long is the delay?

- [ ] 10 cycles
- [x] 20 cycles
- [ ] 30 cycles
- [ ] 50 cycles

::: {.explanation}
30 Å = 1.0 Å × (50 − n~delay~), so n~delay~ = 20 cycles. The apparent GPC from this single film (0.6 Å) would underestimate the true value by 40 %.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A TMA/H~2~O process has a GPC of 1.1 Å, and one layer of Al~2~O~3~ is about 2.9 Å thick. A student concludes that the TMA half-reaction is undersaturated, because a saturated half-reaction should give a full monolayer. What is wrong with this reasoning?

- [ ] Nothing; the TMA dose should be increased until the GPC reaches 2.9 Å.
- [ ] The water half-reaction must be undersaturated instead.
- [x] Saturation means no further uptake, not full coverage. Steric crowding by the remaining methyl groups and the finite –OH density cap a saturated cycle at roughly 30–40 % of a monolayer.
- [ ] GPC is a rate, so it cannot be compared with a layer thickness.

::: {.explanation}
A saturated half-cycle stops when every remaining –OH is consumed or shielded by ligands, which happens well before a full layer of Al is adsorbed [@Barry2022; @Puurunen2005]. Increasing the dose beyond saturation does not raise the GPC.
:::
:::

### Ligands

::: {.quiz}
A precursor loses a neutral ligand in the hot delivery line. Why is this more likely to cause problems than the loss of an anionic ligand?

- [ ] Neutral ligands always have higher bond enthalpies.
- [x] Losing an L ligand leaves a neutral metal fragment that can survive in the gas phase and react unpredictably; losing an X ligand heterolytically would leave a cation that does not survive under reasonable conditions.
- [ ] Anionic ligands cannot be removed by a co-reactant.
- [ ] Neutral ligands are always larger, so they block the surface.

::: {.explanation}
The L/X distinction tells you what fragments a bond cleavage produces. Neutral metal-containing fragments can persist in the gas phase and complicate the chemistry [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Sc–O bonds are more ionic and stronger than Sc–N bonds. What does this suggest for Sc(thd)~3~ compared with Sc(iPrAMD)~3~?

- [ ] Sc(thd)~3~ will decompose at lower temperatures and leave oxygen in the film.
- [x] Sc(thd)~3~ should keep its ligands at intermediate temperatures and lose them by cleanly breaking the Sc–O bond, while Sc(iPrAMD)~3~ is more likely to decompose thermally at another bond and leave nitrogen.
- [ ] Both will behave the same, because both are Sc(III).
- [ ] Ionicity has no bearing on where a bond breaks.

::: {.explanation}
High bond enthalpy resists thermolysis; high ionicity favours clean heterolytic cleavage at the metal under chemical attack. The weaker, more covalent Sc–N bond is more likely to fail elsewhere in the ligand [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Using the data in @tbl-chelate, what happens to the stability advantage of the chelate (en) over two NH~3~ ligands as the temperature rises?

- [ ] It shrinks, because the enthalpies are similar.
- [ ] It stays constant.
- [x] It grows, because the entropy difference (about 31 J K^−1^ mol^−1^) is multiplied by T.
- [ ] It reverses above 400 K.

::: {.explanation}
ΔΔG = ΔΔH − TΔΔS = (−54 + 46) − T(23 + 8.4)/1000 kJ mol^−1^, which becomes more negative as T increases. At 300 K the chelate is favoured by about 17 kJ mol^−1^; at 600 K, by about 27 kJ mol^−1^.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
ZrCp~2~Me~2~ is pulsed onto a hydroxylated surface. Methane is the main by-product, but cyclopentadiene is also detected. Why is CpH released at all, given that CH~4~ (pK~a~ ~50) is far less acidic than CpH (pK~a~ ~16)?

- [ ] The pK~a~ values are reversed at ALD temperatures.
- [ ] Cp ligands are always lost first because they are larger.
- [x] Surface reactions in ALD are not at equilibrium: the leaving ligand is swept away by the gas flow, so less favourable pathways can still contribute.
- [ ] The Cp ligand is lost by thermal decomposition in the source.

::: {.explanation}
pK~a~ predicts which ligand is lost under equilibrium conditions. In ALD, products are removed as they form, so kinetically accessible but less favourable pathways compete. Linking the Cp rings into an *ansa*-zirconocene adds a chelate effect, and then only methyl is lost [@Barry2021].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
The Al(R-ip)Me~2~ compounds with R = ^i^Pr and ^s^Bu decomposed fastest at 78 °C. What did this suggest, and how was the ligand redesigned in response?

- [ ] Carbodiimide deinsertion was still active, so the ring was enlarged.
- [x] β-Hydrogen elimination was still possible, so the ring β-hydrogens were replaced with methyl groups and a tert-butyl group was put on the imine.
- [ ] The Al–Me bonds were too weak, so the methyls were replaced with chlorides.
- [ ] The compounds were oligomerizing, so bulkier R groups were used throughout.

::: {.explanation}
The iminopyrrolidinate ring already blocks deinsertion. The fastest-decomposing compounds were the ones with reactive β-hydrogens, which pointed to β-H elimination. Removing those hydrogens gave [Cu(Me~2~-^t^Bu-ip)]~2~, with no measurable decomposition at 165 °C [@Barry2013].
:::
:::

### Precursors

::: {.quiz}
A gold film is deposited from a Au(III) precursor and ozone. Which statement best describes the role of ozone?

- [ ] Ozone reduces Au(III) to Au(0).
- [ ] Ozone oxidizes Au(III) to Au(V).
- [x] Ozone combusts the ligands; gold, which prefers the zero oxidation state, takes up electrons during the combustion and ends up as Au(0).
- [ ] Ozone is not involved; the precursor decomposes thermally.

::: {.explanation}
The gold is formally reduced, but it is not accurate to call ozone the reducing agent. Labels such as "oxidant" describe what is added, not necessarily what happens to the metal [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Why does adding CF~3~ groups to a dimethylgold(III) β-diketonate increase its volatility?

- [ ] It lowers the molecular weight.
- [ ] It raises the enthalpy of vaporization.
- [x] Fluorine is hard to polarize and holds its electrons tightly, which weakens intermolecular interactions and lowers the enthalpy of vaporization.
- [ ] It makes the compound decompose at a lower temperature.

::: {.explanation}
CF~3~ is heavier than CH~3~, so molecular weight cannot be the explanation. Volatility is controlled by intermolecular interactions in the condensed phase [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A precursor is a free-flowing powder at room temperature and is delivered from a solid source at 120 °C. Over many runs, the dose delivered by a fixed pulse slowly falls. What is the most likely cause?

- [ ] The precursor's enthalpy of sublimation increases over time.
- [x] The surface area of the solid shrinks as particles evaporate, and impurities collect on it, so the evaporation rate drops.
- [ ] Solids always have lower vapour pressures than liquids.
- [ ] The carrier gas becomes saturated.

::: {.explanation}
A liquid presents a constant surface and keeps impurities mobile; a solid does not. This is why a melting point between handling and source temperature is useful [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
In MeAlCl~2~, which ligand is expected to react with a surface hydroxyl, and why?

- [x] The methyl group, because CH~4~ is a far weaker acid than HCl, so CH~3~^−^ is the stronger base.
- [ ] A chloride, because Al–Cl bonds are more ionic.
- [ ] Both equally, because they are on the same metal.
- [ ] Neither; the compound physisorbs.

::: {.explanation}
The ligand whose conjugate acid has the highest pK~a~ is the strongest base and the most likely to accept a surface proton. The chlorides remain on the chemisorbed aluminum [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
In DMAI, [Me~2~Al(O^i^Pr)]~2~, which ligand is expected to react first with a surface hydroxyl, and what does that predict for the GPC compared with TMA?

- [ ] The isopropoxide, because Al–O bonds are more ionic; a higher GPC.
- [x] A methyl, because CH~4~ is a much weaker acid than isopropanol; the isopropoxide stays on the surface fragment, which is bulkier, so a lower GPC.
- [ ] Both at once; the same GPC.
- [ ] Neither; DMAI only physisorbs.

::: {.explanation}
The ligand whose conjugate acid has the higher pK~a~ is the stronger base and is protonated first. A retained isopropoxide makes each chemisorbed fragment larger, so steric saturation sets in at fewer Al per nm^2^ (@sec-tma-dmai).
:::
:::

### Thermolysis

::: {.quiz}
A new precursor is run by TGA at 10 °C min^−1^. With 10 mg in the pan, the residual mass is 1 %; with 50 mg it is 9 %. What does this tell you?

- [ ] The balance is drifting; the two results should be averaged.
- [ ] The larger sample evaporated faster.
- [x] The compound decomposes slowly at the temperatures reached late in the run. A larger sample stays in the pan longer and at higher temperature, so more of it decomposes. It is a risk in a source held hot for days.
- [ ] The compound is a solid, so the result is meaningless.

::: {.explanation}
This is the thermal stress test. The evaporation rate is set by the pan area, so more mass means more time at temperature. A clean precursor gives the same, near-zero residue at every mass [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A candidate has T~V~ = 90 °C, T~D~ = 180 °C, a TGA residue of 3 % and a payload mass fraction of 30 %. What is its figure of merit σ?

- [ ] 90 °C
- [x] 81 °C
- [ ] 87 °C
- [ ] 63 °C

::: {.explanation}
σ = (T~D~ − T~V~)(1 − %m~r~/%m~M~) = 90 × (1 − 3/30) = 81 °C (@eq-fom).
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
The Me~3~AuPMe~3~/H~2~ plasma process gave saturating growth up to 120 °C, but its safe upper limit was later revised to 100 °C. Why?

- [ ] The precursor decomposes in the source above 100 °C.
- [ ] The H~2~ plasma etches gold above 100 °C.
- [x] Above 100 °C, the methyl and phosphine ligands left on the gold surface start to desorb during the precursor pulse, freeing sites for more precursor, so growth is no longer limited by the surface.
- [ ] The film becomes amorphous above 100 °C.

::: {.explanation}
In situ studies showed ligand loss during the exposure itself [@VanDaele2020]. The decomposition was catalysed by the gold surface; it would not have been predicted from TGA or DSC of the precursor (@sec-au-120).
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A new aluminium precursor (M = 450 g mol^−1^, 6.0 % Al) loses 28 % of its mass in a first TGA step at 110–180 °C, holds a plateau, then loses the rest above 230 °C with no residue. What is the best reading?

- [ ] A clean precursor: there is no residue.
- [ ] It decomposes to aluminium metal; the plateau is the metal.
- [x] It loses a fragment of about 126 g mol^−1^ (for example a carbodiimide) and the product evaporates. The vapour that reaches the reactor is not the compound that was loaded.
- [ ] The first step is solvent, and the second is the precursor.

::: {.explanation}
28 % of 450 g mol^−1^ is 126 g mol^−1^, the mass of ^i^PrN=C=N^i^Pr. A plateau at 72 % is far above the 6 % that aluminium (or the 11 % that Al~2~O~3~) could account for, so the plateau is a new molecule, not a residue. Zero residue does not prove a clean precursor (@sec-tga-decomposition).
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
In an isothermal TGA hold, precursor A loses mass in a straight line to 0 %. Precursor B loses mass quickly at first, then more and more slowly, and levels off at 25 %. Which statement is right?

- [ ] Both are evaporating; B simply has a lower vapour pressure.
- [x] A is evaporating from a fixed pan area (constant rate). B's rate falls as it is consumed, which is the behaviour of a reaction, and its plateau is a non-volatile product.
- [ ] A is decomposing, because its mass reaches zero.
- [ ] B is the better precursor because some of it remains for the next run.

::: {.explanation}
Evaporation from a fixed area is zero order in sample mass, so the line is straight. A first-order decomposition gives a curve that slows down and ends on a plateau at the residual mass (@sec-tga-decomposition).
:::
:::

### Mechanisms and surfaces

::: {.quiz}
When ozone reacts with a surface Al–CH~3~ group to give Al–OCH~3~, which fundamental step is this?

- [ ] Oxidative addition
- [ ] Reductive elimination
- [x] Migratory insertion: the methyl moves from aluminum onto the newly bound oxygen.
- [ ] Disproportionation

::: {.explanation}
The oxidation state of aluminum does not change; the methyl migrates onto oxygen, which looks like insertion of O into the Al–C bond [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Why can a copper ALD precursor not carry two ligands that could reductively eliminate from each other, even though reductive elimination is what produces Cu^0^ in the process?

- [ ] Reductive elimination only happens on oxide surfaces.
- [x] The precursor would then decompose to the metal by itself, continuously, which gives CVD rather than self-limiting growth. The eliminating pair has to be assembled at the surface, after chemisorption and a ligand exchange.
- [ ] Two such ligands would make the precursor non-volatile.
- [ ] Copper cannot change its oxidation state at ALD temperatures.

::: {.explanation}
In the Cu(dmae)~2~/ZnEt~2~ process, ethyl groups are put on surface copper by exchange with ZnEt~2~, and only then eliminate butane [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Which hydrogen-terminated surface is expected to react with TMA as a *hydride* (H^δ−^) rather than as a proton?

- [x] Ti–H, because titanium (χ = 1.54) is less electronegative than hydrogen (χ = 2.20).
- [ ] Pt–H, because platinum is a noble metal.
- [ ] Au–H, because gold binds hydrogen strongly.
- [ ] None; surface hydrogen always behaves as a proton.

::: {.explanation}
Hydrogen bonded to a less electronegative element carries a partial negative charge. Noble metals, W and Pb polarize the bond the other way, so their surface hydrogens are protic [@Barry2022].
:::
:::

## Further reading

- @Barry2022, Chapters 2–7: saturation, ligands, precursors, thermolysis, nucleation and surface mechanisms; the main source for this chapter.
- @Puurunen2005: the definitive case study of TMA/H~2~O surface chemistry and of GPC-limiting factors.
- @Barry2021: the main organometallic precursor families and their surface mechanisms.
- @Richey2020: a review of chemical and physical mechanisms in ALD, and of where the textbook mechanisms break down.
- @Barry2013: a case study in designing a ligand against specific decomposition pathways.
- @Griffiths2016 and @VanDaele2020: gold ALD from Me~3~AuPMe~3~, from the first process to the mechanism that revised its window.
- @Leskela2003: a classic review of ALD chemistry and precursor selection.
- @Knisley2013 and @Emslie2013: precursors and reducing chemistry for metal films, the hardest case.
- @Profijt2011: plasma-assisted ALD and how plasma second precursors differ from thermal ones.
- @Puurunen2004 and @Gladfelter1993: growth modes in the first cycles, and selectivity as a matter of nucleation rates.
- @George2010 and @Johnson2014: broad overviews of ALD chemistries and mechanisms.
